title: Proposal: engineer-facing technical documentation as part of feature acceptance
body:
﻿FieldCraft already requires cited numerical methods and reproducible verification tests. However, mathematical explanations are scattered across developer-oriented documents and Rust source comments.

**Proposal:** make documentation intended for engineers, not Rust developers, part of the **definition of done** for each new or significantly changed analysis capability declared ready for use.

A concise, versioned technical reference should cover:

1. **Theory:** physical assumptions, governing equations, defined notation, reasons for the chosen formulation, applicability and limitations.
2. **Verification:** links to reproducible oracle cases, published references, convergence checks and known failures.
3. **User guidance:** inputs, units, a worked example and interpretation of results.
4. **Publication and languages:** documentation delivered with the corresponding release, prepared for translation and available in the languages required for its intended markets.

Ideally, implementation, verification and source-language user documentation should be reviewed in the **same PR**. Experimental features can remain explicitly labelled as such.

A lightweight, reusable template/checklist would be a practical first step; there is no need to rewrite the existing documentation.

**Principle:** an engineer must be able to understand and assess a numerical method **without knowing or reading Rust**.

title: Fluid: walls where the surface is (interpolated bounce-back) for curved obstacles
body:
### Current behaviour

The lattice puts every obstacle wall half way between a fluid cell and a solid one, so a curved
wall is a staircase. On Schäfer & Turek's 2D-1 cylinder that costs about 1.3 % of drag on 20 cells
across it, and in a Poiseuille pipe it is the error that dominates (L2 4.5e-2 at 4 cells per radius,
9.5e-3 at 16).

### What you need and why

Drag and pressure drop on curved parts (cylinders, ducts, fins) within about 1 % of the
reference without very fine grids.

### Expected behaviour

An option on the fluid domain, `walls: halfway | interpolated | quadratic` (default `halfway`, so
nothing changes unless asked), that puts each wall link's bounce-back where the obstacle's surface
really crosses it, linear and quadratic (Bouzidi, Firdaouss & Lallemand 2001). The crossing comes
from the obstacle's triangle tree (a segment–triangle test, Möller & Trumbore 1997). CPU and GPU
(the GPU runs the linear one). Heat keeps its walls half way (the curved conducting interfaces are
#631).

Two findings from trying it, in case they matter elsewhere:

- `schafer_turek_2d1_cylinder_drag_and_lift` runs 10 time units, about one viscous time D²/ν at the
  cylinder. The wake is still settling then, and the drag reads several percent high for every wall
  and collision. At 40 units the half-way TRT cylinder on 20 cells is c_D 5.655 (+1.3 %) instead of
  5.773 (+3.4 %), and Δp (extrapolated to the surface) is inside the interval.
- An interpolation's cells behind a link have to wrap across periodic faces; otherwise a case one
  cell deep takes half its links half way.

Measured on a working branch (settled 2D-1, 20 cells across the cylinder):

| Case | Half-way | Interpolated | Quadratic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Poiseuille pipe, L2, 4 cells/radius | 4.5e-2 | 6.6e-3 | 3.4e-3 |
| Poiseuille pipe, L2, 16 cells/radius | 9.5e-3 | 6.5e-4 | 7.7e-4 |
| 2D-1 c_D (ref 5.57–5.59) | 5.655 (+1.34 %) | 5.610 (+0.54 %) | 5.598 (+0.32 %) |
| 2D-1 Δp (ref 0.1172–0.1176) | 0.1172 | 0.1168 (−0.5 %) | 0.1163 (−0.9 %) |

GPU checked on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Laptop GPU (Windows, DX12/Vulkan via wgpu): the
interpolated sphere matches the CPU to 3.4e-6 in velocity and 2.4e-6 in drag.

I'd like to take this one, with a PR against `develop`.

### References

- M. Bouzidi, M. Firdaouss, P. Lallemand, *Momentum transfer of a Boltzmann-lattice fluid with
  boundaries*, Phys. Fluids 13, 3452 (2001).
- T. Möller, B. Trumbore, *Fast, minimum storage ray-triangle intersection*, J. Graphics Tools 2(1)
  (1997).
- M. Schäfer, S. Turek, *Benchmark computations of laminar flow around a cylinder* (1996).

title: GPU: user-selectable backend (Vulkan default on Linux/Windows, Metal on macOS; others 'coming soon')
body:
Native GPU support is Vulkan only, per the owner decision following #708. #561 and #708 are closed as superseded; no DXC packaging or manual DX12 setup is planned.

Implement the policy consistently across the desktop viewport, offscreen rendering, GPU fluid solves and GPU meshing:

- Remove native D3D/DX12, Metal and OpenGL backend selection and DXC/FXC compiler handling.
- Disable transitive native backend features as well as direct ones; keep the browser's WebGPU/WebGL build working.
- Keep Vulkan hardware/software adapter selection and process/device reuse. Unsupported backend overrides must never select a different native backend; strict GPU requests should fail actionably and headless auto rendering may retain its CPU fallback.
- Update diagnostics, platform/support documentation and verification guidance. Do not present historical Metal/DX12 measurements as current support.
- Validate the touched crates, native Cargo feature graph and supported software/hardware Vulkan paths; record unavailable platform/hardware checks honestly.

This is backend support cleanup. The fan/porous GPU work (#705 / #698), buffer splitting (#699) and coupled exchanger (#700) remain separate work.

title: Proposal: NAFEMS Test 51 and FV5 modal oracle benchmarks
body:
## Proposal from @flexcut

I would like to contribute **reproducible NAFEMS free-vibration verification cases** to `tests/oracle/`. The models were constructed and solved directly with **FieldCraft v0.7.0 on Windows** from published problem descriptions, without using or extracting inputs from any commercial CAE program.

I am opening this issue before proposing a PR, in accordance with `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

### NAFEMS Test 51 — deep simply-supported *solid* beam

Primary source consulted: *Selected Benchmarks for Natural Frequency Analysis* (NAFEMS, 1987), Test 51 (original printed benchmark sheet). Dimensions L=10 m, section 2×2 m, E=200 GPa, Poisson ratio 0.3, density 8000 kg/m³.

Boundary conditions in local coordinates: u_x′=u_z′=0 on edge AA′; u_z′=0 on edge BB′; u_y′=0 on side y′=2 m. Consistent mass matrix. The published discretizations were recreated using FieldCraft's `mesh.block`.

| Mode | NAFEMS f_r (Hz) | FieldCraft 5×1×1 HEX20 (Hz) | DIANA published HEX20 (Hz) | FieldCraft 10×1×3 HEX8 (Hz) | DIANA published HEX8 (Hz) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 38.200 | 38.268448 | 38.268 | 40.721333 | 40.721 |
| 2 | 85.210 | 87.659445 | 87.659 | 88.663649 | 88.663 |
| 3 | 152.230 | 157.492124 | 157.49 | 164.333322 | 164.33 |
| 4 | 245.530 | 259.003128 | 259.00 | 275.220148 | 275.22 |
| 5 | 297.050 | 306.010243 | 306.01 | 306.629679 | 306.63 |

Independent published source: [DIANA verification manual, NAFEMS free-vibration cases 51hx20 and 51hx8b](https://manuals.dianafea.com/d103/Verify/Verifyse6.html), tables 3.75 and 3.77.

**Critical qualification:** The original NAFEMS sheet distinguishes reference values `f_r` from discretization-specific test results `f_t`. The FieldCraft results reproduce the published DIANA frequencies for the two meshes, **not necessarily the NAFEMS continuum/reference frequencies**. Additional refinement (HEX20 10×2×2 and 20×3×3; HEX8 20×2×6 and 30×4×6) produced decreasing frequencies, some below `f_r`; this is an **open investigation**, not a proven solver bug or a reason to enlarge the tolerance. Further controls included rotating the entire model and its local boundary directions (frequencies unchanged to 6 decimal places) and comparing consistent/lumped mass and HEX8 incompatible-mode variants.

### NAFEMS Test 5 (FV5) — 1-D deep simply-supported beam

Same 10 m length, square 2×2 m section and material. `beam2` Timoshenko elements; consistent-mass mesh refinement (5, 10, 20, 40, 80 elements), plus a 5-element lumped-mass run. At 80 elements:

| Mode(s) | FieldCraft (Hz) | Published NAFEMS target (Hz) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1–2 bending | 42.645149 | 42.650 |
| 3 torsion | 71.197230 | 71.200 |
| 4 axial | 125.002008 | 125.000 |
| 5–6 bending | 148.159113 | 148.150 |
| 7 torsion | 213.619141 | 213.610 |
| 8–9 bending | 283.535920 | 283.470 |

Reference cross-check: [ANSYS/LS-DYNA verification manual, VM-LSDYNA-SOLVE-064](https://ansyshelp.ansys.com/public/views/secured/corp/v261/en/lsdyna_vm/vm-lsdyna-solve-064.html). Independent analytical checks were made for 125 Hz axial quarter-wave and the Saint-Venant torsional modes (~71.196 and ~213.588 Hz). The original Test 5 sheet was unavailable in the hardcopy inspected, so this published secondary source would be cited explicitly.

### Contribution proposal

- Original FieldCraft `recipe.json`, a source-cited `expected.json` with justified tolerances, and a short README documenting geometry, BCs, element formulation, modal ordering, convergence evidence and limitations.
- Produce `fixture.json` using `cargo xtask oracle --case` and `--bless` **only after** a passing test, and regenerate `docs/oracle.md`.
- No copying of NAFEMS/vendor page images, model decks, text or commercial software outputs. Only published numerical target values with attribution.
- Keep mesh-specific regression verification separate from the unresolved continuum-reference investigation.

Would the maintainers welcome these cases? In particular, would you prefer separate HEX8/HEX20 oracle directories for Test 51, and FV5 in a subsequent PR?

— @flexcut

title: 0.7.5: reproducible heat-exchanger tutorials and release videos
body:
## Goal
The maintainer requests videos that help people use 0.7.5 to model flow and heat transfer in a heat exchanger. Deliver tutorials from reproducible release samples, not only a promotional animation.

## Proposed series
- [ ] **Your first heat exchanger (8–12 min):** geometry and fluid passages, materials, conducting wall, inlet/outlet and fan/pump or prescribed-flow assumptions, resolution, resource estimate, solve and save. Start from a supplied model/recipe.
- [ ] **Where does the heat go? (3–5 min):** velocity/temperature sections and streamlines, both outlet temperatures, heat duty, pressure loss and mass/energy budgets from the same solved model.
- [ ] **Choose a fan and compare fin spacing (5–8 min):** one controlled design change, fan/system operating point, cooling benefit versus pressure drop, and comparable convergence/resolution.
- [ ] **Can you trust this result? (about 5 min):** validation reference, refinement, convergence of running means for LES, uncertainty and model limits.

## Definition of done
- Inputs/recipes, exact version/commit, solve settings, hardware/runtime and saved outputs accompany each video; a viewer can reproduce the result.
- Captions and legends show physical units and distinguish measured numerical results from assumptions.
- Air-side-only examples are labelled as such. A full exchanger tutorial requires demonstrated coupled coolant/air support.
- A physical transient is labelled with physical time; accelerated steady-state heat-capacity runs and iteration playback are never presented as physical warm-up.
- No use of commercial CAE assets or models; original SolidCraft geometry and the repository's capture workflow.
- Publish gallery links, a thumbnail/hero still and a short release clip only once the final results and commands match the release build.

Related tooling: `tools/cooling`, `tools/flow-clip`, and `docs/examples.md`. The existing `cooling-aio` airflow clip is a starting point, but its held-temperature/air-side assumptions must remain visible.

title: 0.7.5: specify and verify coupled air/coolant heat-exchanger domains
body:
## Goal for 0.7.5
Model flow and heat transfer in a heat exchanger with distinct hot/cold fluid passages and a conducting separator. The existing AIO sample solves only the air side with an assumed coolant temperature; neither a drawn tube nor two independent solves represents a coupled liquid-to-air exchanger.

## Source audit (develop 7d9c027d71)
- `FluidDomain` has one fluid `material` (`crates/model/src/fluids.rs`). Multiple domain definitions are allowed.
- `Setup::new` selects a single fluid step/domain; `solve_fluid_on` builds one `Flow` and runs its backend (`crates/lbm/src/setup.rs`, `solve.rs`).
- Conducting obstacles exchange heat with that domain's fluid. I found no orchestration that exchanges the wall state/flux between different fluid solves.
- CPU/GPU CHT (#609/#651) and thermal contact resistance (#677) therefore provide necessary pieces, but do not establish two-fluid coupling.

## Specify before implementation
- [ ] Choose the minimal supported exchanger: separate air/coolant circuits, fluid properties, geometry/wall thickness and prescribed flows or fan/pump conditions. Record whether the first accepted case is laminar or turbulent and why.
- [ ] Document domain ownership/occupancy, shared wall identity, conservative interface transfer, units, coupling iterations, under-relaxation, time stepping and stopping criteria. A shared wall's heat capacity/source must not be counted twice.
- [ ] Define support for steady vs transient runs and CPU/GPU combinations. Accelerated solid heat capacity may be used only with explicit steady-state semantics.
- [ ] Specify result/probe/export and save/reopen semantics for both circuits and the shared wall; reject unsupported combinations explicitly.

## Acceptance evidence
- [ ] A simple two-stream exchanger matches a cited analytical energy-balance/effectiveness reference at stated tolerances, with independently computed hot/cold heat duties and mass-flow-weighted outlet temperatures.
- [ ] Energy and mass budgets expose imbalance and external losses/sources, rather than hiding disagreement in a single reported duty.
- [ ] Spatial and coupling-tolerance refinement, pressure-drop checks, a closed/insulated energy test where applicable, and an existing single-domain regression suite.
- [ ] One reproducible cooling/exchanger model runs through the normal commands and UI and saves/reopens both sides' results. No hidden manual flux handoff.

The first deliverable is the coupling specification and a minimal reference case; implementation should be split into reviewable changes from that evidence. This is a single-phase two-fluid/domain workflow, not a request for multiphase/free-surface physics.

title: 0.7.5: split GPU population buffers beyond the per-buffer cell limit
body:
## Problem
The maintainer identified this as urgent for 0.7.5 in #642. The GPU currently allocates all 19 momentum populations in one storage buffer and rejects `4 * 19 * cells` above the device's per-buffer cap (`crates/lbm-gpu/src/native.rs`, `GpuFlow::with_options`). At a 2 GiB cap this is about 28 million cells, below the intended fine cooling grids even when total GPU memory is sufficient. #678 fixed overall solve caps, not this buffer layout limit.

## Scope
Split population storage into device-supported buffers while preserving the AA in-place and AB streaming paths, boundary handling, thermal/solid coupling and collision options. Choose the layout using actual device limits, checked arithmetic and a documented addressing scheme. Do not replace the limit with a larger fixed assumption.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Small grids match the existing layout (bit-for-bit when arithmetic order is unchanged; otherwise explain and justify the numerical tolerance) and CPU within existing tolerances, for both collisions and AA/AB, with and without heat/conducting solids.
- [ ] Test addressing and streaming across every buffer split, including boundary links; exercise a deliberately small test cap without allocating multi-GiB fixtures in normal CI.
- [ ] Include LES and fan/porous integration when those branches land; maintain device binding-limit checks.
- [ ] Memory estimates account for the actual buffer layout, staging, thermal fields, host state and requested output frames; impossible allocations fail before creating buffers and explain the limiting resource.
- [ ] Demonstrate a real-hardware case above the former per-buffer cell limit and report cells, memory, throughput and CPU-reference comparison on a smaller version.
- [ ] Preserve wasm builds and actionable errors for adapters that cannot support the layout.

Related: #642, #650, #678, #665. The maintainer offered this work to @bluecmd in #642; no implementation is claimed by filing this issue.

title: 0.7.5: GPU fan curves and porous resistance zones
body:
## Problem
For 0.7.5's heat-exchanger/electronics-cooling workflow, the fan operating point and vent/filter resistance must work on the GPU-sized models. CPU support landed in #596. `GpuFlow::with_options` currently rejects any `Flow::zones()` entry (`crates/lbm-gpu/src/native.rs`). The maintainer requested this as a separate PR in #642.

## Scope
Port the existing CPU fan pressure–flow curves and Darcy–Forchheimer/loss-coefficient porous zones through the existing backend/commands. CPU remains the reference. Keep reductions and fan feedback on the device where practical; quantify any readback cost. Preserve the CPU force/velocity convention, including the implicit porous velocity correction and fan relaxation timing.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Porous pressure drop agrees with the analytical cases already used by #596 and with CPU at stated f32 tolerances, including strong resistance and both supported collisions/streaming layouts.
- [ ] Fan plus resistance reaches the analytical curve/system operating point; record flow, curve pressure rise and measured rise/drop with the existing histories/replies.
- [ ] A heated conducting-solid case runs with both fan and porous zones; zone momentum forcing and thermal buoyancy compose correctly.
- [ ] Model with no zones retains existing GPU results; unsupported/hostile zone combinations fail by name before device work.
- [ ] Respect per-kernel device binding limits and memory estimates; GPU/CPU comparisons and a real-hardware throughput measurement are recorded in the PR.
- [ ] Run the resulting fan-driven cooling/exchanger acceptance case and update the CPU-only limitation in docs.

Related: #642, #661, #665. This was offered to @bluecmd in #642; it is not assigned to a new contributor by this issue.

title: 0.7.5: heat-exchanger and electronics-cooling release acceptance
body:
## Goal
0.7.5 is the electronics-cooling release discussed in #584. The maintainer has asked us to focus on modelling flow in a heat exchanger, reach feature completeness for that workflow, and propose videos that help people use it. This issue collects release acceptance and dependencies; it does not claim unverified capabilities are complete.

## Verified baseline (develop 7d9c027d71, 2026-10-23)
- CPU and GPU conjugate heat transfer, conducting solids with component power and orthotropic conductivity: #609, #651.
- Thermal TRT: #679; component temperature limits: #676; thermal contact resistance: #677; machine-bounded solve caps: #678.
- Fan curves and porous resistance on CPU: #596. GPU still refuses both in `crates/lbm-gpu/src/native.rs`.
- Natural-convection oracle cases at Ra 10³–10⁶ are present with recipes and fixtures. Remaining electronics validation is tracked in #623.
- The existing `cooling-aio` sample is air-side only, with a held radiator temperature. It is not a solved water loop or a coupled two-fluid exchanger.

## Release acceptance
- [ ] Finish the CPU LES work (#663/#664, PR #668) and GPU port (#665, PR #692), including statistically steady monitoring and the stated numerical verification. Stability alone is not validation of turbulent heat transfer.
- [ ] GPU fan curves and porous resistance, checked against CPU and an analytical operating point (#698).
- [ ] GPU population-buffer splitting and accurate memory estimates, with a representative large run (#699).
- [ ] Specify and close the air/coolant coupling gap for the heat-exchanger target: distinct fluid properties, separate flow paths, conservative transfer through the conducting wall and convergence of both sides. Separate independent solves do not satisfy this acceptance case (#700).
- [ ] Complete forced-convection/heat-sink validation in #623 and record a refinement study relevant to the exchanger; curved-interface uncertainty remains visible (#631).
- [ ] Supply a reproducible exchanger model/recipe: geometry, properties, boundary conditions, fan/pump or prescribed-flow assumptions, mesh/cell spacing, time step, convergence settings and hardware/runtime.
- [ ] Report hot/cold inlet and mass-flow-weighted outlet temperatures, heat duty on both sides, pressure losses, flow rates, mass/energy imbalance and numerical uncertainty. Choose and record justified tolerances with the benchmark specification before freezing reference results.
- [ ] Save and reopen the solved model and its views without solving again (#682), and generate labelled temperature/velocity sections, streamlines and a result summary from the same saved run.
- [ ] Refresh the cooling gallery and release-facing documentation: current capabilities, physical approximations and measured numbers, with no obsolete “CHT is missing” or “old collision ceiling” claims.
- [ ] Publish reproducible tutorial/video inputs and outputs (#701). Clips must distinguish physical transients from accelerated steady-state iteration.

## Related work / boundaries
The blower-cooled card (#642, draft #661) exercises the same GPU/LES/fan path and remains useful acceptance evidence; it does not replace the two-fluid exchanger check. Remote (#568/#411), broad structural features and general UI cleanup are outside this release's critical path unless they block the demonstrated workflow. The curved-wall algorithm change in #631 remains parked as previously agreed; the accuracy measurement is still relevant.

This tracker records current source/issue evidence, not a new full runtime verification. Open technical decisions and missing evidence should remain unchecked.


## Backup-maintainer pass, 2026-10-23

Issue tracking is reconciled on #157, #623, #642, #664 and #665. #632 now records its outstanding screenshots/macOS/X11/Wayland review evidence; Remote #568 remains deliberately parked.

Reviews posted:
- CPU LES #668: changes requested for missing averaged statistics in the command reply, omitted LES host memory in the estimator, and the multi-hour ignored test entering a 60-minute heavy CI job. Local verification: 84 model + 16 LBM library tests and six short turbulence tests pass. Physical statistical-convergence and final cooling acceptance remain open.
- GPU LES #692: changes requested for chunk-dependent eddy-viscosity diagnostic semantics; existing CPU-dependency and CHT/GB10 acceptance still apply. Three library/WGSL checks and the four-combination software-Vulkan Re=5000 cavity comparison pass. This is not hardware performance evidence.
- Meshing gate #670: commented review; seven independent validity-unit tests pass, but its last full heavy run is red. Rebase onto current develop and revalidate the two topology failures after #687 before approving.

First follow-up fix: #702 / PR #703 requests the Claim bot's explicit PR-write permission. All 52 existing bot tests pass locally. It needs core-maintainer review/merge and an upstream retrigger to establish whether the original #692 HTTP 403 is cleared. The change does not resolve the LES solver review findings.

title: Epic: explicit dynamics for beams, shells and 2D structural elements
body:
### Current behaviour

FieldCraft's explicit solver supports one-point hex8 solids, nodal-pressure tet4 solids, and rod2/rod3 trusses, with formulation restrictions. Its element gate rejects beams, shells and general 2D continuum elements. Existing truss support does not provide beam bending or shell behaviour.

### What you need and why

Run transient structural analyses of slender members, thin-walled parts, and plane or axisymmetric sections with suitable structural elements. These models need bending, rotational inertia, thickness treatment or 2D kinematics that the current explicit element set does not provide.

### Expected behaviour

Extend explicit dynamics in separately reviewable element-family increments. Each increment must define its supported kinematics, materials, loads, constraints, contact and output, rather than assuming that every implicit capability transfers automatically.

Implementation work to split into linked child issues:

- [ ] **Beams:** translational and rotational dynamics, section stiffness and inertia, applied moments, and the chosen finite-rotation treatment.
- [ ] **Shells:** membrane and bending response, director/rotation updates, thickness integration and rotational inertia, with stabilization where the formulation needs it.
- [ ] **Plane continuum elements:** plane stress and plane strain, with an explicit support table for element orders and material formulations.
- [ ] **Axisymmetric continuum elements:** radial/axial kinematics, hoop terms, consistent mass and force integration, and treatment of nodes on the symmetry axis.

Shared acceptance criteria for each increment:

- [ ] Use a documented formulation derived from published literature; specify lumped mass/inertia and a justified stable time-step estimate.
- [ ] Verify rigid motion and the small-deformation limit. Finite-rotation or finite-strain support requires separate objectivity tests.
- [ ] Demonstrate mesh and time-step convergence against analytical or published structural benchmarks: beam vibration/bending, shell plate vibration or transient bending, plane wave propagation, and an axisymmetric radial response as appropriate.
- [ ] Report kinetic and internal energy, external work, and any stabilization or dissipative terms consistently. Check energy and momentum balances on applicable unloaded cases.
- [ ] Support the declared loads, boundary conditions and result fields through the existing command and result workflows.
- [ ] Document contact eligibility and mixed-element compatibility. Refuse unsupported combinations explicitly.
- [ ] Preserve the existing explicit solid and truss verification cases and deterministic CPU behaviour.

### References

- [Explicit solver element/formulation gate](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/explicit/src/system.rs), `check_formulation`.
- [FieldCraft element families](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/elements.md).
- [FieldCraft roadmap](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/ROADMAP.md), explicit dynamics and shells milestones.

title: Nonlinear mechanics: finite-rotation reference-point couplings
body:
### Current behaviour

In nonlinear static analysis, FieldCraft's reference-point couplings retain the linear solver's small-rotation constraints and emit a warning. The surrounding solid can undergo finite deformation, but a coupled reference point cannot correctly impose a large rigid rotation on its attached region through those linear constraints.

### What you need and why

Apply loads and prescribed motion through a rotating fixture or end attachment. Examples include bending a flexible part through a large angle and rotating the loaded end of a deformable tube. A rigid rotation of the attachment should not introduce artificial deformation or stress into a region intended to move rigidly.

### Expected behaviour

Add finite-rotation kinematic reference-point couplings for nonlinear static steps, with a documented rotation representation and frame convention. Update the constraint equations and their consistent linearization as the configuration changes, and report reference-point reactions using the same convention.

Start with kinematic couplings. Finite-rotation distributing couplings should be specified separately because their load distribution and admissible deformation need their own treatment. Explicit-dynamics couplings are outside this request.

Acceptance criteria:

- [ ] A stress-free body driven through a finite rigid translation and rotation by a reference point preserves distances and develops no spurious strain or stress within a stated numerical tolerance.
- [ ] Rotation is supported about an arbitrary axis, including a sequence of rotations about different axes; document composition and prescribed-rotation semantics.
- [ ] In the small-rotation limit, results recover the existing linear coupling behaviour.
- [ ] A deforming cantilever or tube with a rotating end attachment passes a cited analytical or published benchmark with a mesh-convergence study.
- [ ] Reference-point forces and moments balance the corresponding nodal resultants in the documented configuration and frame.
- [ ] Check the linearization numerically and demonstrate nonlinear convergence on a smooth finite-rotation case; rejected increments restore the committed coupling state.
- [ ] Existing commands, saved models and results consistently express the new behaviour. Unsupported partial constraints or incompatible combinations are rejected explicitly.

### References

- [FieldCraft nonlinear mechanics documentation](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/fem.md): the Couplings paragraph documents the current small-rotation restriction.
- [FieldCraft element and degree-of-freedom framework](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/elements.md).

Select and cite the finite-rotation constraint formulation from published mechanics literature before implementation; each verification case should state its reference and tolerance.

title: Linear buckling: initial-stress stiffness for beams, shells and trusses
body:
### Current behaviour

FieldCraft's linear buckling solver builds initial-stress stiffness for solid and 2D continuum elements. It refuses beams, shells and trusses because their initial-stress stiffness is not implemented. Those structural element families are already available for linear static and frequency analysis.

### What you need and why

Assess the stability of beam frames, thin shell structures and prestressed pin-jointed assemblies using their structural meshes. A model that can be solved for its linear preload should be usable for an eigenvalue buckling analysis when its element formulations support that analysis.

### Expected behaviour

Extend the existing buckling procedure with formulation-consistent geometric stiffness for beams, shells and trusses, assembled from the preload state. Preserve the existing load-factor and mode-shape workflow, including mixed meshes where the supported elements share degrees of freedom.

For trusses, the feature is assembly stability and prestress effects: an axial-only truss does not acquire bending stiffness or represent the local flexural buckling of an individual member.

Contact-preloaded buckling needs a separate specification of the contact state and its linearization and is outside this request. Nonlinear postbuckling is also a separate procedure.

Acceptance criteria:

- [ ] Derive and document each element family's geometric stiffness from published theory, including its kinematic assumptions and supported preload states.
- [ ] Beam column critical loads and mode shapes converge to closed-form results for at least two end conditions; account for shear deformation where relevant.
- [ ] A simply supported shell plate under in-plane compression converges to its analytical buckling load and mode.
- [ ] A pin-jointed assembly reproduces an analytically derived prestress-dependent tangent or instability condition, without attributing bending resistance to truss members.
- [ ] Mixed supported-element models assemble consistently; rigid modes and insufficient constraints produce useful diagnostics.
- [ ] Existing solid and 2D buckling cases retain their documented accuracy. Each new reference case records mesh convergence and a justified tolerance.
- [ ] Document supported element/formulation combinations and make unsupported combinations fail by name.

### References

- [FieldCraft: linear buckling](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/fem.md#linear-buckling).
- [FieldCraft element families](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/elements.md).
- Follow-up to #87. Separate from the buckling result-type work in #174.

title: [Feature Request] Animations should update contour colours across steps
body:
### Current behaviour

As in title, the existing animation features show changes in deflection but not changes in the contours (stress, etc) across an animation.



### What you need and why

My use case for animations is to see how stress "flows" through a mechanical part from load = 0 to load = full when the part is complex. In other words, I see how the stress contours in a part vary from the beginning to the end of an animation.

title: Topology optimisation (M22): minimum compliance with SIMP, checked against published optima
body: ### Current behaviour FieldCraft can mesh and solve a part's design space, but nothing tells you where the part needs its material. ROADMAP M22 lists topology optimisation (SIMP with filters) as planned; there is no issue for it yet. ### What you need and why Design a part in SolidCraft, find where it needs material under its loads and supports, and take the result back to SolidCraft as a shape to rework, without leaving the two apps. That is the classic minimum compliance problem: the stiffest layout of a static step within a volume limit. ### Expected behaviour I have this working on a branch rebased on develop (11 commits, not pushed yet), built while the tet mesher fixes in #687 were under way: tet-meshing parts for this work is where the folds of #666 turned up. Before I open a pull request, I'd like to know whether you want it, and in one pull request or several. What it does: - **`solve.topology`** (Solve › Topology): minimum compliance of a linear static step under a volume fraction. Modified SIMP, optimality criteria with bisection on the volume, and two filters: the Helmholtz PDE filter (the default; one factorization, so its cost does not grow with the radius) and the classic cone density filter. A design set, sets kept solid where loads go in and supports hold (`keep`, and `keep_thickness` for a wall of given depth behind a face), a warning when a kinematic coupling sits on the design. The same result bit for bit on any number of threads. - **Results**: the density as a contour field, the void left out of the view with an adjustable cutoff, a `density` cell array in the VTU export, and the design's surface as a closed STL (marching tetrahedra, Taubin smoothing with the part's own faces kept), which SolidCraft inserts as a mesh body (`file.insert_mesh`). A 120 × 40 × 30 mm block optimised to 30 % of its volume comes back into SolidCraft as a closed body of 28 %. - **A gallery sample**, `mbb-beam`: an aluminium MBB beam that optimises into the familiar truss in about 2 s. How it is checked: four oracle cases reproduce published optimum compliances of the same problems (same mesh, element, interpolation, filter and stop rule): | Case | Source | Published | FieldCraft | |---|---|---|---| | MBB beam, 60 × 20, cone filter | Andreassen et al. 2011, Fig. 3 | 233.71 | 233.7099 | | MBB beam, 60 × 20, PDE filter | Andreassen et al. 2011, Fig. 4 | 237.60 | 237.6002 | | MBB beam, 150 × 50, PDE filter | Andreassen et al. 2011, Fig. 4 | 235.36 | 235.3637 | | Cantilever, 160 × 80, 500 iterations | Amir, Aage, Lazarov 2014, Table 2 | 84.36 | 84.3609 | Checked by hand as well, and left out of the oracle for CI time: the 150 × 50 beam with the cone filter (235.73: 235.7348), the 300 × 100 beam with both filters (238.31 and 236.62: 238.3150 and 236.6225) and Wallin et al.'s 40 % beam (315.8: 315.84). The 88 line paper gives the filter radius of its 300 × 100 mesh as 16; its own rule (0.04 times the width) gives 12, and 12 is the radius that reproduces its printed compliances, so 16 looks like a misprint. Not in it yet: several load cases, MMA, projection (Heaviside) filters, manufacturing constraints, and meshing the optimised design to solve it again. ### Pictures The `mbb-beam` sample after Solve › Topology with half its volume: density contours with the void left out. ### References - M. title: Tet validity gate: a per-edge winding check
body:
### Current behaviour
With the fixes for #666, `tet::linear_gate` refuses tetrahedra joined to the mesh by vertices alone, faces held by more than two tetrahedra, and a listed boundary other than the faces held once. It also compares the mesh's volume with what its boundary encloses. An over-wound edge, where the tetrahedra round an edge cover more than a full turn, overlaps without any face held three times, and for positive tetrahedra the summed volume is the winding-weighted volume the boundary encloses, so the volume test passes it as well.

### What you need and why
A gate that certifies the mesh does not overlap itself before the solver sees it, whatever operation made the overlap.

### Expected behaviour
For every edge, the dihedral angles at that edge of the tetrahedra round it sum to 2π for an interior edge and to less than 2π for a boundary edge, within a stated tolerance; the gate refuses the mesh otherwise and names the first edge and where it is. Floating point is fine in a gate, as the volume test is. This also covers a face held by three tetrahedra.

### References
None beyond the geometry: in a mesh that does not overlap itself, the tetrahedra round an interior edge fill exactly one full turn, and those round a boundary edge less than one.

title: Tet mesher: an exact swept-face check in place of the 30° boundary turn bound
body:
### Current behaviour
With the fixes for #666, a move of a boundary vertex in the tet quality stage (smoothing, ODT, the final snap) is refused when one of its boundary faces turns by more than 30° (`BOUNDARY_TURN_COS`, `turns_over`, the bound `collapse` already kept), or when one of its moved faces meets another boundary face in more than their shared vertices (the skin index). The 30° bound stands in for an intersection question:
- it is measured from where the vertex is when it moves, so successive passes can turn a face further;
- it is a floating-point threshold where the rest of the checks are exact;
- in a thin slot, where the interior angle at an edge is close to 360°, a fold needs less than 30°;
- the face-to-face skin test cannot see a fold across a shared edge: two triangles sharing an edge meet properly unless they lie in one plane on the same side.

### What you need and why
An exact check, depending only on the mesh, that no move or change folds the skin, including across an edge two boundary faces share.

### Expected behaviour
- A boundary vertex `v` moving from `x` to `p` sweeps, for each boundary face `(a, b, v)`, the tetrahedron `(a, b, x, p)`. A move is valid when each swept tetrahedron meets every other boundary face (not holding `v`) in their shared vertices alone, by an exact simplex test such as the facet recovery's `cdt::meet::meet_properly`, which already takes a tetrahedron and a triangle.
- `TetComplex::replace` does the same at each edge shared by a removed and a made boundary face: `(a, b, v_0, v_{m−1})` for an edge removal's 2-2 flip, `(p, q, a, b)` for a collapse, `(edge, old apex, new vertex)` for an insertion.
- The 30° bound then goes, or stays as a documented limit on how far a face may turn for shape fidelity, like `BOUNDARY_FLIP_COS`, not as the fold guard.

### References
- L. Diazzi, D. Panozzo, A. Vaxman, M. Attene, *Constrained Delaunay Tetrahedrization: A Robust and Practical Approach*, ACM TOG 42(6):181, 2023, §4.4: simplices meeting properly, as the facet recovery tests them.
- J. R. Shewchuk, *Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates*, DCG 18:305–363, 1997.

title: Desktop: file dialogs block the UI thread, so Wayland compositors flag FieldCraft as not responding
body:
### Observed failure
On Hyprland (Wayland), pressing Ctrl+S opens the save chooser (`xdg-desktop-portal-gtk`) and the compositor shows an **Application Not Responding** warning for FieldCraft on top of it. Reported by @MayberryDT in a partial Omarchy / Hyprland pass on the v0.7.0 Linux tarball (#100, Intel HD Graphics 500, Vulkan).

### Cause (from the code)
The desktop app opens its file dialogs with `rfd::FileDialog` (`apps/fieldcraft/src/main.rs`, the `dialog(...).save_file()` and open calls), which is synchronous: the call blocks the UI thread, and so the event loop, until the chooser closes. While the portal's chooser is open the window stops answering the compositor's pings, and Hyprland (like GNOME's mutter) flags the app as not responding. The web build already uses `rfd::AsyncFileDialog`.

### Expected behaviour
The event loop keeps running while a file chooser is open: no "not responding" warning, the window keeps repainting, and the dialog's result is applied when it arrives. Use `rfd::AsyncFileDialog` (or run the blocking dialog off the UI thread) for open, save, save-as, import and export, with the result delivered back to the app; the dialogs stay UI-only (programmatic commands never open dialogs).

### Reproduction
Linux on Wayland (Hyprland 0.56.2 here; GNOME should show the same), `fieldcraft --sample cantilever`, press Ctrl+S, leave the chooser open for a few seconds.

title: Tet mesh: boundary nodes added by refinement stay on the tessellation's facets, so curved faces never get closer than the chordal tolerance
body:
### Observed failure

In a tet mesh refined below the tessellation's own facet size, the boundary nodes that refinement adds lie on the **tessellation's flat facets**, not on the design's curved faces. Refining therefore never brings the boundary closer to the true surface than the chordal `tolerance`. Stress peaks on small fillets keep changing with refinement instead of converging. In a convergence study of a printed part, fillet peaks rose about 10 % per refinement step.

### Reproduction

A block with a Ø10 bore and a 0.3 mm fillet round the bore's top edge, with a 0.06 mm size control around one point of the fillet:

```json
[{"command":"solid.box","params":{"corner":[0,0,0],"length":30,"width":30,"height":10,"body_name":"Block"}},
 {"command":"solid.cylinder","params":{"diameter":10,"height":10,"base":[15,15,0],"axis":"Z","operation":"cut","targets":["Block"]}},
 {"command":"solid.fillet","params":{"edges":[[20,15,10]],"radius":0.3}}]
```
(saved with `solidcraft-cli run design.json --save design.solidcraft`)

```json
[{"command":"geometry.open","params":{"path":"design.solidcraft"}},
 {"command":"mesh.size.set","params":{"name":"Round","size":0.06,"sphere":{"center":[20.3,15,9.7],"radius":1}}},
 {"command":"mesh.tet.generate","params":{"tolerance":0.05,"size":2}},
 {"command":"mesh.export.stl","params":{"path":"skin.stl","format":"ascii"}}]
```

Then measure each boundary node's distance from the exact surface, within 1 mm of (20.3, 15, 9.7):
- the fillet is a torus, centre circle radius 5.3 at z = 9.7, tube radius 0.3;
- the bore is a cylinder of radius 5.

### Evidence

| Face | Boundary nodes | Distance from the exact surface: median | 95th percentile | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 mm fillet (`solid.fillet`) | 205 | 0.0000 mm | 0.0155 mm | 0.0178 mm |
| Ø10 bore (cylinder face) | 224 | 0.0000 mm | 0.0217 mm | 0.0275 mm |

The median is exact (the tessellation's own vertices), but the nodes refinement adds in between sit on the facets, up to the chordal sag. On a 0.3 mm fillet, 0.018 mm is 6 % of the radius, which is a geometric corner at every facet edge. Without the size control (a 1 mm fillet, global size 0.25) almost every node was exact, with one or two up to 0.02 mm.

### Expected behaviour

Boundary nodes, and the mid-side nodes of tet10, lie on the exact face. They'd be projected onto the B-rep face as `mesh.node.relax` already slides surface nodes on the geometry (#398), and as the projection blocking mesher does (#399). Refinement then converges to the true shape, whatever the tessellation `tolerance`.

### Investigation

Lowering `tolerance` to 0.01 works around it, but roughly doubled the element count in the larger study, and the error is still bounded by the tessellation, not the mesh. I haven't checked whether tet10 mid-side nodes are placed on the surface; `mesh.export.stl` writes corner nodes only.

### Version and platform

FieldCraft develop 7160a82 (CLI); design saved by SolidCraft 0.16.2; Linux (Ubuntu 24.04).

title: Lattice Boltzmann: Smagorinsky subgrid closure (LES) on the CPU
body:
**Why.** Without a turbulence model the lattice solver needs cell Reynolds numbers below roughly 30–40 (u·Δx/ν; the regularised collision at τ ≈ 0.508). Real cooling flows break that on any grid we can hold. The graphics card of #642 diverges with only 0.5 m/s into its intake on 0.5 mm cells: a jet in the 1.9 mm gap between the VRM blocks and a fin stack's base plate reaches a cell Reynolds number of about 90, at the same step on the CPU and the GPU (details on #642 and #661). A subgrid closure is the standard way lattice Boltzmann reaches such speeds on practical grids.

**What.** A Smagorinsky eddy viscosity in the CPU lattice solver (`crates/lbm`), opt-in per fluid step.
- **Momentum:**
  - ν_t = (C_s Δ)² |S|, with the strain rate taken locally from the non-equilibrium momentum flux each cell already has. The regularised collision computes `P = Π^neq + ½(uF + Fu) ≈ −2ρ c_s² τ S`.
  - That makes the relaxation time a per-cell closed form with no extra neighbour access: τ = ½(τ₀ + √(τ₀² + 18√2 C_s² |P| / ρ)), in lattice units, from S. Hou, J. Sterling, S. Chen, G. D. Doolen, *A lattice Boltzmann subgrid model for high Reynolds number flows*, Fields Inst. Commun. 6:151–166, 1996.
  - Built on the recursive regularised collision, as in O. Malaspinas, P. Sagaut, *Consistent subgrid scale modelling for lattice Boltzmann methods*, J. Fluid Mech. 700:514–542, 2012.
- **Heat:** with a thermal lattice, the turbulent diffusivity α_t = ν_t / Pr_t (Pr_t ≈ 0.85–0.9) is added to the scalar lattice's relaxation per cell. Otherwise the temperature lattice runs at the same high cell Péclet numbers. That means one stored ν_t (or τ) per fluid cell.
- **Model and commands:** a step setting, for example `"turbulence": {"type": "smagorinsky", "constant": 0.1, "prandtl": 0.9}` (or a collision value), with reply fields for the largest eddy viscosity ratio ν_t/ν. Off by default, so every current result stays bit for bit. The TRT collision refuses it clearly, or it's defined for TRT too.
- Cited in the module docs and in the literature list. No code of any LES or lattice Boltzmann package is read.

**Verification (docs/verification.md, `tests/oracle/` where it fits):**
- Off: all current tests and fixtures unchanged.
- Laminar: Poiseuille or Couette, where |S| is known, gives the closed-form ν_t, and the profile follows the effective viscosity.
- Taylor–Green decay: the energy decays at the effective viscosity's rate.
- A case the plain scheme can't hold (a lid-driven cavity or channel at high cell Reynolds number) stays stable, with a published reference where one fits.
- Heat: a heated channel where α_t follows ν_t / Pr_t.
- Hostile parameters: a negative, huge or NaN constant is refused.

**Done when** the CPU solver runs the #642 card (0.36–0.5 mm cells, 2–3 m/s into the intake) to steady state with the closure on, and the checks above pass.

The GPU port is a separate issue. Part of #642's path to real fan speeds; related to #157.

title: Diagnostics for solver failures that aren't panics, and for headless runs in throwaway environments
body:
### Current behaviour

Crash reports (docs/crash-reports.md) cover panics and unclean exits well: message, backtrace, replay, renderer, GPU and driver. Two kinds of failure leave nothing behind:

1. **Solver failures that aren't panics.** A GPU device lost mid-session (#636: `GPU: Parent device is lost` from the 11th device in one process on one NVIDIA driver, the 26th on another) and a fluid solve stopped by GL's storage-buffer limit (#640) both come back as an ordinary `invalid input` error. No report says which adapter, backend, driver and limits were in use, how many devices the process had opened, or where the step was. The same goes for a diverged solve, a solve stopped by its caps, or an out-of-memory failure.
2. **Headless runs in throwaway environments.** `fieldcraft-cli mcp` or `run` under automation writes to `fieldcraft-automation/` in the temporary folder. In a container removed after the run, or on a cloud instance (#411), that folder goes with it. `FIELDCRAFT_CRASH_DIR` helps once you know it exists, but nothing points a worker to it, and the CLI prints no path when it writes one.

### What you need and why

To tell a FieldCraft bug from an environment problem after the fact, especially on remote workers where no one watched the run. #636, #640 and #643 each needed a manual reproduction to recover information the failing run could have recorded itself.

### Expected behaviour

- A solver error that stops a solve writes a small diagnostic record (not a crash report), next to the crash reports or under `FIELDCRAFT_CRASH_DIR`. It holds:
  - the command and its parameters, the model's size (cells or DOFs), and the step and increment or time reached;
  - the backend and adapter: name, driver, backend type (Vulkan, GL, Metal, DX12, CPU), and the limits that matter (storage buffers per stage, max buffer size);
  - for GPU runs, the devices and instances this process has opened;
  - the error;
  - and, if a checkpoint exists, its path.

  `diagnostics.crash_reports` could list these too, with `kind: "solver_error"`.
- Headless runs print the path of any report or record they write, on stderr and in the MCP reply.
- `docs/crash-reports.md` gets a short note for workers: set `FIELDCRAFT_CRASH_DIR` to a persistent folder in containers and on cloud instances.

### Pictures

None.

### References

#636 and #641 (device loss), #640 (GL limit), #643 (CPU scaling), #411 (remote and cloud workers).

title: Checkpoint and resume long solves (fluid, explicit, nonlinear, transient heat)
body:
### Current behaviour

A solve runs to the end or is lost. When the process stops partway (killed to free a machine, an out-of-memory kill, a lost GPU device, a reboot, a closed SSH session), nothing of the run survives: the next attempt starts again from step 0. The solve commands have no checkpoint, restart or resume option.

Real case: a CPU `solve.fluid` of the `cooling-enclosure` sample took 2,124 s. A run of the larger `cooling-aio` sample was about two hours in when the machine had to be quietened, and all of it was lost. On the GPU the same samples take seconds to a minute, but long fine-grid or long-time fluid runs, explicit dynamics and long nonlinear solves are just as exposed.

### What you need and why

To run long solves on a shared or remote machine without betting the whole run on the process surviving. That's the case #411 plans for: a cloud instance that's terminated by a cost cap, a spot interruption or a watchdog must be able to resume its job, not repeat it. The same holds for the desktop: an app restart shouldn't throw away an overnight run.

### Expected behaviour

A long solve can write its state now and then and later carry on from it, with the same result as an uninterrupted run, since FieldCraft is deterministic:
- Steps that advance in time or increments (fluid, explicit, nonlinear static, transient heat) write a checkpoint every N steps or minutes. A checkpoint holds the populations and macroscopic fields, or the displacements, velocities and state variables, plus the step counters and the frames already written. Writing should be atomic, as model saves already are.
- A solve started on a model whose step has a checkpoint from the same model and solver settings offers to resume, or `solve.* {"resume": true}` does it. A checkpoint from changed settings is refused with a message.
- `solve.*` reports `checkpoint_every` and the last checkpoint, and keeps or deletes checkpoints when the run ends.
- A resumed run gives bit-identical results to an uninterrupted one on the same backend and thread count, which a test can check like the existing determinism tests.

### Pictures

None. This is about how a run is executed, not what it shows.

### References

Restart files are a standard part of long-running solvers. In lattice Boltzmann, a checkpoint is simply the population arrays (and the thermal arrays) at a step.

title: CPU fluid solver stops scaling at ~4 threads (flow-past: 1.5× at 4, slower at 64)
body:
### Observed failure

The CPU lattice Boltzmann solver barely speeds up past 4 threads, and gets slower at 64. Wall time of `solve.fluid {"backend": "cpu", "threads": N}` on the `flow-past` sample (184,320 cells, 3,200 steps), one MCP session, the sample reopened before each solve:

| threads | 1 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| solve (s) | 49.0 | 32.4 | 35.1 | 34.9 | 33.9 | 44.0 |
| speed-up | 1.0× | 1.5× | 1.4× | 1.4× | 1.4× | 1.1× |

That's about 12 million cell updates per second on one thread and at most 18 on many. The same sample on the GPU backend (a recent NVIDIA GPU, Vulkan) takes 3.9 s.

### Reproduction

```sh
fieldcraft-cli mcp
```

then for each N, `execute` `file.sample {"name": "flow-past"}` and time `execute` `solve.fluid {"backend": "cpu", "threads": N}`. A `fieldcraft-cli run` script with the same two commands shows the same plateau.

### Evidence

Machine: a 64-thread x86 server, Ubuntu 24.04 in Docker, otherwise idle (load average 2.9 when the run started). FieldCraft `develop` afb7543, release build. A laptop (12 threads) solves the same sample in about 35 s, the same as the 64-thread machine.

### Expected behaviour

Close to linear scaling up to the memory bandwidth limit. At 184k cells and 19 f32 populations the two lattices are about 28 MB, which fits in this CPU's cache, so many more than 4 threads should help.

### Investigation

From reading `crates/lbm/src/flow.rs` and `crates/parallel` (not profiled):
- **Few, small work items.** The lattice is split into blocks of `CELLS = 4096`, which is only 45 blocks on this grid. Each block holds a fraction of a millisecond of work. Each step runs several rayon passes over them (collide, stream, open boundaries…), and through `with_max_len(1)` each block is its own task. With 3,200 steps that's tens of thousands of fork-joins of 45 tiny tasks, so scheduling and the join barriers can dominate as threads are added. That would also explain 64 threads being slower than 32.
- **Serial parts per step.** Anything outside the parallel passes in `Flow::step` (the max-speed reduction, open boundaries, the force sums, frame capture) caps the speed-up (Amdahl). A profile would show how much that is.

Things that might help: smaller blocks when the grid is small (so there are many items per thread), or fusing collide and stream into one parallel pass per step. Determinism doesn't need to change, since the fixed partition can stay fixed.

### Version and platform

FieldCraft `develop` afb7543 (CLI and MCP server, built from source, release). Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04 container), a 64-thread x86 server.

title: Example: a blower-cooled 2-slot graphics card (conjugate heat transfer)
body:
## Current behaviour
The electronics-cooling examples (#587) hold their solids at a fixed temperature, because conduction inside solids only arrived with #609. None of them shows heat starting as a component's power and travelling through real solids into air driven by a fan.

## What to build
A flagship example: a generic, 2-slot, blower-cooled high-end graphics card, about 267 × 111 × 40 mm. It is our own design, with no vendor's layout, logo or branding.

- **Geometry (SolidCraft recipe):**
  - a PCB with a GPU package, memory chips and VRM blocks;
  - a copper base on the die and heat pipes;
  - a dense aluminium fin stack along the card;
  - a shroud with a fan opening, and a radial blower impeller visible through it;
  - a backplate;
  - an I/O bracket with exhaust slots.
- **Physics (release target, CPU reference and GPU):**
  - The die, memory and VRMs are conducting solids with power: about 250–300 W on the die, 2–3 W per memory chip, 20–30 W across the VRMs.
  - The copper base, heat pipes (orthotropic, high k along their axis), fins and FR-4 board (orthotropic) are conducting solids too.
  - The blower is a fan zone with a pressure–flow curve (#596). The bracket slots are a porous vent, and the exhaust a convective outlet (#626).
  - Use the regularised collision (#627) with the LES work in #663/#664/#665 for the practical-grid speeds that diverged without it; case air at 35–40 °C intake, and steady runs with the solids' heat capacity scaled (#609).
  - The impeller is visual only: there is no rotating geometry in the solver, and the docs will say so.
- **Outputs:**
  - The die's peak temperature, plus the base, fin, memory and VRM temperatures.

title: First window: keep the restored or cascaded position inside the work area (second monitor, 125 % cascade)
body:
### Observed failure

Two cases where the first window's position, not its size, puts part of it off the work area. Both were left open by #601 / #607.

**1. 125 %: Windows' cascade pushes a window that fits under the taskbar.** At 125 % on a 3440 × 1440 monitor the default 1400 × 900 points (1750 × 1125 px) fits the 1380 px work area, so #607's fit doesn't apply and Windows places the window. Its default placement cascades each new window by about 32–38 px. In the #607 Windows check, one launch on develop opened at (288, 288) px (frame bottom 1413 px) and one launch of #607's commit at (320, 320) px (frame bottom 1445 px), both below the 1380 px work area. The command line and the journal timeline are behind the taskbar until the window is moved. Other launches opened at 32–224 px and fit.

**2. A second monitor (from @jyviko's review of #607).** When the first window doesn't fit, #607 computes its size from the window's current monitor (`viewport().monitor_size`). But it sends `OuterPosition` in desktop coordinates measured from the origin, as if that monitor's top-left were (0, 0). When the window opens on a monitor that isn't at the desktop's origin (on macOS a new window can open on a smaller secondary screen), that position moves it onto the primary monitor with a size computed for the other one.

### Reproduction

Case 1, Windows 11, one 3440 × 1440 monitor at 125 %, no saved window state:

1. Start `fieldcraft.exe` with no arguments several times in a row (with a few seconds between launches; each launch cascades further).
2. Watch the bottom of the restored window: once the cascade offset passes about 255 px, the timeline strip is under the taskbar.

Case 2: from the code. `fit_first_window` in `apps/fieldcraft/src/main.rs` sends `ViewportCommand::OuterPosition(fit.min)` whatever monitor the window is on.

### Evidence

Case 1, 125 %, the #607 build launched at (320, 320) px. The screenshot is cropped at the work area, so the command line is cut and the timeline is hidden:

![125 % cascade](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bluecmd/fieldcraft/issue-evidence/601/windows-125-cascade-320.png)

Measured with `GetWindowRect`/`GetClientRect` in a DPI-aware process: window (320, 320)–(2070, 1445) px, client 1400 × 900 pt, work area (0, 0)–(3440, 1380) px. The full table is in the Windows check comment on #607.

### Expected behaviour

The first window is fully inside the work area wherever the system places it, on the monitor it opens on:

- When the default size fits but the system's placement would put the window past the monitor less the reserve, move it up/left just enough (or to the top, centred across) so that it fits.
- Send a position only when the window opened on the monitor at the desktop's origin, where positions from the monitor's top-left are also desktop positions. Elsewhere, send only `InnerSize` + `Maximized` and leave placement to the system, as @jyviko suggested.

### Investigation

winit gives the current monitor's size but not its origin or work area, so both cases use the same test: is the window's top-left within `[0, monitor)`? Note that this can't be "is the outer rectangle inside the monitor": in the #601 case the window cascades to about (202, 202) pt with 900 pt of height on a 960-pt monitor, so its rectangle isn't inside, yet that's exactly where the position is needed.

The second-monitor part is written and tested on our side (`at_origin_monitor`, a pure function with its own test, `cargo test -p fieldcraft` and clippy clean). The 125 % clamp would reuse the same test and the existing reserve. We'd like to take this one, as one small PR, with the same Windows check (125 % cascade ×3, 150 % regression) before marking it ready.

### Version and platform

develop at 9c8ab0e (after #607), Windows 11 Pro 26200, RTX 4090, release build; case 2 from @jyviko's review on macOS.


## Outstanding review evidence (2026-10-23)

PR #633 has Windows cascade and two-monitor measurements, but the maintainer's last review still requests:

- [ ] Paired before/after screenshots showing the clipped timeline/taskbar and corrected placement.
- [ ] macOS: a first window that already fits keeps the system's position.
- [ ] Linux X11: the same placement check.
- [ ] Linux Wayland: unknown-position handling leaves placement to the system.

Keep this open until those checks are supplied and #633 is reviewed/merged. This is outside #697's cooling critical path unless it blocks the demonstrated workflow.

title: Conjugate heat transfer: accuracy at curved conducting interfaces (staircase)
body:
## Current behaviour
Conjugate heat transfer (#609) couples a conducting solid to the fluid across the lattice's cell faces, so a curved interface is a staircase. On Rayleigh's square array of cylinders (r = 0.3, conduction only, against the Perrins–McKenzie–McPhedran series at the voxelised area fraction), insulating inclusions (k_s/k_f = 0.1) show the staircase as a first-order error: −3.85 / −2.23 / −0.85 % on 16 / 32 / 64 cells. Conducting ones (k_s/k_f = 10) stay within 0.3 %. Curved heat-sink fins with convection have not been measured yet.

## What to build
1. Measure: a convective case with curved conducting interfaces and a published reference, e.g. a heated or conducting circular cylinder in cross-flow or in an enclosure, with Nusselt numbers from the literature, on three grids.
2. If the staircase costs accuracy there too, put the interface flux on the true surface: cut cells, or an interpolated (curved) interface treatment for the scalar lattice. #597 found that cut cells fixed the same loss on the Eulerian-solid branch.

The tests in `crates/lbm/tests/conjugate.rs` (`a_square_array_of_cylinders_conducts_as_rayleigh_s_series`, `insulating_cylinders_converge_at_first_order`) are the starting point.

title: SolidCraft 0.16 renames split and blend faces: keep old models' references working
body:
Tracking issue for the face, edge and vertex renames that come with SolidCraft 0.16, which #613 (the #605 fix) adopts.

## What happened
FieldCraft refers to design geometry by SolidCraft's persistent names (`F9:face:4`, `F2:side:l4|F9:face:4`). Sets, seeds, size controls, mesh plans, virtual faces, fluid faces and the mesh's own face tags all store these names.

SolidCraft 0.11, FieldCraft 0.7.0's pin, could not trace a face produced by some operations (splits, blends). It named those faces by position, as the k-th face of the feature, and marked the names `exact: false`. SolidCraft 0.16 traces them and names them by their origin:

| 0.11 name (positional) | 0.16 name (from history) | What the face is |
|---|---|---|
| `F9:face:4` | `F9:section` | the cut face made by split F9 (plane y = 16) |
| `F10:face:4` | `F10:section` | the cut face of split F10 |
| `F7:face:12` | `F7:section` | the cut face of split F7 |
| `F9:face:7` | `F3:blend:F2:side:l3\|F2:side:l4` | the fillet F3 between those two sides |

The B-rep is identical: same faces, areas and centroids, and volumes agree to 1e-13. Only the labels change. SolidCraft's format steps v23–v27 contain no rename map, because the change is in the naming algorithm, not the file format. Its old namer is `pub(crate)`. SolidCraft's own references survive because they store a point with each name and fall back to the nearest face; FieldCraft's references store no point.

## Measured exposure (corpus, committed designs, all 12 samples, Pi 5 enclosure; 33 sources)
| Design | Faces renamed |
|---|---|
| `filleted-bracket-blocks` / sample `bracket-hex` (same geometry) | 108 of 190 (57 %) |
| `crank-arm` / `crank-mirror` | 9 of 58 |
| `pi5-enclosure` | 33 of 687 |
| every other corpus part, hollow-box and open-tray fixtures, other samples | 0 |
| **Total** | **267 of 1592 faces**; 862 of 3625 edges; 652 of 2398 vertices |

- Every renamed face was an `exact: false` positional name. No old name was reused for a different face.
- Each of the 267 matches exactly one new face by centroid and area, with zero difference.
- Committed references that go stale: none. No fixture, sample set or oracle recipe points at a split face, which is why no test caught this.
- **Who is exposed:** user models made with 0.4–0.7 that reference faces, edges or vertices of split, partitioned or filleted bodies.

## Impact without a fix
A 0.7.0 model with a set, load or seed on `F9:face:4`:
1. Opens with no warning, and `model.check` reports nothing, because the old mesh still carries the old tags.
2. A remesh silently drops the seed.
3. `model.check` then says only "set `cut` resolves to nothing on the current mesh", without naming the face.

## Fix in #613
- **Never silent:** opening checks every stored reference against the design and reports stale ones by name. A remesh warns for each seed or size control it could not apply. `model.check` names the vanished face.
- **Rename on open, when a mesh exists:**
  - The mesh facets tagged with the old name are sampled (centres, plus corners pulled halfway in) and located on the new tessellation.
  - A name is renamed only if every sample lands on one face, the areas agree within 5 %, and no other stale name lands there.
  - Edges and vertices are remapped through their face pairs.
  - Every rename is listed in the open reply and the status line, and the model is marked changed so the user saves it deliberately. Opening writes nothing.
  - Ambiguous matches are refused and reported, never guessed.
- **No mesh:** references are reported stale with "pick it again".
- **Regression guard:** a golden list of the split bracket's 870 names, plus a daily job that opens designs saved by the latest SolidCraft release. A future rename fails a test until someone approves it.

## Remaining work
- [ ] #613: independent re-review of rename-on-open (congruent mirrored pieces, partly meshed faces, tolerances, faces partitioned in FieldCraft, plans, fluid faces, all 267 corpus renames, undo after open, cost on large meshes)
- [ ] #613: rebase after #603, re-take the relaxation fingerprint, full Linux CI run
- [ ] **Durable references:** store a witness point (and area) with every face, edge and vertex reference, so future renames resolve through SolidCraft's `face_on_body(body, name, point)` without a mesh. This is a model-format addition, so it follows #603's format 3.
- [ ] Release notes for 0.7.1: designs from SolidCraft 0.16 open; faces of split or filleted bodies have new names; meshed models are migrated on open (listed), unmeshed ones report the references to pick again.

Related: #605, #613, #603, #579.

title: Node relax amplifies a 1-ulp input change into node moves of up to 2 mm
body:
### Observed failure
Node relaxation turns a 1-ulp change in its input mesh into node movements of up to about 2 mm. Its output is not a continuous function of its input.

### Reproduction (on develop 93eff2ef)
1. Open the drop-test sample and generate its mesh.
2. Perturb every node coordinate by 1 ulp (for example, mm → m → mm, which is inexact for 6–18 % of mesher-computed coordinates).
3. Run the same guarded `mesh.node.relax` on both meshes and compare.

1644 nodes differ by up to 0.735 mm. On the other samples, guarded relax moves 90–99 % of nodes by 0.18–1.87 mm (crank 1.87, ibeam 1.26, heated-bracket 0.8, rubber-seal 0.26), and strong relax moves them by up to 1.09 mm (crank). Each run is deterministic; only the 1-ulp input changes.

### Expected behaviour
A relaxation whose result is stable under round-off: a 1-ulp input change moves nodes by round-off, not by tenths of a millimetre. The likely causes are discrete decisions taken on near-ties (guards, accept/reject tests, ordering by quality) or an iteration that stops on a threshold. Both turn round-off into a different path.

### Why it matters
With SI storage (#603), every mesher sees the mm image of stored metres. Relaxing a model again, or replaying a 0.7 journal that relaxes, can therefore give a mesh up to about 2 mm away from 0.7's. Stored models are unaffected. The same sensitivity also means a relaxed mesh depends on details as small as the order of operations.

Found while reviewing #603.

title: Research: Eulerian solids on the lattice (reference map technique) and LBRMT coupling
body:
Research track from the LBM–FEM coupling review: solids described on the fixed lattice instead of a separate FEM mesh.

**Method.** The reference map technique (Kamrin, Rycroft et al.) stores in every cell the reference position ξ(x,t) of the material there, advected with the material velocity (∂ξ/∂t + v·∇ξ = 0). The deformation gradient is F = (∇ξ)⁻¹, so finite-strain constitutive laws (neo-Hookean etc.) give the Cauchy stress on the grid; a level set marks the solid. The lattice Boltzmann variant (LBRMT) couples such solids to an LB fluid on the same grid with one velocity field: no separate mesh, no interface mapping, no coupling iteration.

**Plan (each step its own PR):**
1. `docs/research/reference-map.md`: citations, links, and our own summary of the method and its open problems (extrapolating ξ into uncovered cells, level-set reinitialisation, stability). Papers kept locally, never committed (copyright).
2. A solid-only Eulerian RMT prototype, verified against known elasticity problems with analytic answers, before any fluid coupling.
3. LBRMT: couple to the existing LBM (CPU first), verified on an FSI benchmark (e.g. Turek–Hron FSI2), compared with the coupled-FEM route.

**Verification problems for step 2:** rigid rotation and translation (zero stress, ξ exact); homogeneous uniaxial stretch and simple shear of a neo-Hookean block (closed-form Cauchy stress); the small-strain limit against linear elasticity; a cantilever or thick-walled cylinder under load against FieldCraft's FEM; wave speed √(μ/ρ) in a bar.

Clean-room: implemented from the published papers only, not from any authors' code.

error: step 1 (geometry.open): invalid input: not a readable design: this design was saved by a newer SolidCraft (file format 26; this version reads formats up to 21): update SolidCraft to open it

title: octree: padding and pillow layers are crushed where the core is a fraction of a cell from a planar face
body:
Part of #85. Found while working on the flattened boundary-layer hexes (crank #190, `stepped-block`, `bolted-assembly`).

## What crushes the padding and pillow layers

Two causes, measured on `stepped-block` and on the `bolted-assembly` clamp, with each worst element's starting and final positions dumped and sectioned:

1. **Wall thickness was read only at triangle centres.** A planar face is a few large triangles. Beside the stepped block's pocket, the x = 60 face's triangles report the wall their centres face (60 mm), while the wall next to the pocket is 5 mm. Those cells stayed at the root size (3.1 mm) while the pocket side was refined to 1.04. The core in the wall came out notched, the notch quads were labelled with the x = 60 patch, and the fit dragged their pads 2 to 6 mm and folded them (4 uncertified elements, then the 250 000-cell retry cap).
   **Fix on branch `octree-85b`** (commit 18569155, with a `needs_split` regression test): on a triangle larger than the cell, the wall is also measured where the triangle is nearest the cell. That reading is held to the plan's thinnest wall, because without the clamp the sharp wedge refines to `max_depth` toward its blade. With it, `stepped-block` meshes (52 274 hexes, min SJ 0.076, volume error -2.7e-6). Every other corpus part is identical except `bolted-assembly`.

2. **The gap between the core and the surface sets the layer thickness, and it can be 0.3 of a cell.** The core keeps `core_offset` (0.3) of its own cell size from the surface. On a planar face aligned with the grid, the gap has the same value all along the face, anywhere in [0.3e, 1.3e). The pad and the pillow share that gap, so at 0.3e each starts about 0.15e thick against e wide. On the clamp body (3 mm wall between the hole and the y = 20 face), fix 1 correctly refines the wall to 0.52 mm cells. The gap at y = 20 is then 0.16 mm, the layers start 0.08 mm thick, and the convex edge y = 20 / z = 5 crushes one element (`bolted-assembly`: "1 elements fail the certified validity check" on all 4 builds). Before fix 1, that wall was meshed at 1.57 mm (under 3 cells across the wall), which is why it passed.
   The gap also jumps by about one coarse cell at every level change along the surface, and the fit shears the layers across that step.

The crank (#190, size 4, defaults) fails the same way, on develop and with fix 1: "1 elements fail the certified validity check" on all 4 builds, about 27 CPU minutes.

## Tried, and why each is not the fix

| change | bolted-assembly | stepped-block |
|---|---|---|
| develop | 41 344, min SJ 0.323 | fails (4 uncertified) |
| fix 1 | fails (1 uncertified) | 52 274, min SJ 0.076 (after a map-failure rebuild, 65 686 cells) |
| fix 1 + `core_offset` 0.45 | 20 168, 0.140 | 4 674, 0.0003 (coarse 3.1 mm cells leave up to 4.5 mm gaps; the map drags vertices) |
| fix 1 + `core_offset` 0.6 | 18 968, 0.025 | 4 240, 0.069 |
| fix 1 + floor from the largest cell sharing a vertex | 21 040, 0.013 | 52 274, 0.076 |
| compass repair also sliding patch and curve vertices | — | no change (elements are folded, not just flat) |

## What is needed

Gap control in the boundary stage, not another constant. The gap that holds the two layers has to be bounded relative to the cells next to it (about [0.5e, 1.5e)), the same on both sides of a level change, and small relative to nearby features. That means one of:
- grading the cells that meet the surface, so a level change happens a few cells inside rather than at the surface;
- placing the core boundary per patch rather than by a per-cell distance floor (for example, dropping the last core layer where the gap is under half a cell, with a topology check);
- Maréchal-style projection of the core boundary followed by the buffer layer.

Fix 1 should land together with that work, not before it: on its own it trades `stepped-block` for `bolted-assembly`.

The corpus numbers above were measured on develop at 85b117ec (before #435 and the libm change). The branch is rebased onto 5db21aba, and its octree tests pass.

title: EM field modelling (conformal antennas, propagation paths) and scripting (Python, time-dependent cases, drone aero)
body:
Two requests from @naturalmechanics, restated with where FieldCraft is today.

## 1. Electromagnetic field modelling — conformal antennas and propagation paths

**Wanted:** full-wave EM on 3D geometry to design/verify antennas conformal to a structure (radiation pattern, gain, input impedance/S11, coupling), and propagation along a path (path loss, rain attenuation).

**Today:** not available. The roadmap only mentions low-frequency electromagnetics later (M19).

**What it would take:**
- a full-wave solver on the existing grids or meshes: FDTD (Yee) on voxelised geometry, or vector (Nédélec) finite elements on the meshes, with absorbing boundaries (CPML), lumped/waveguide ports, far-field transform, S-parameters;
- materials: permittivity, permeability, conductivity, frequency-dependent dispersion;
- propagation: ray tracing over terrain or a scene, with ITU-R models for gaseous and rain attenuation (e.g. P.838) and free-space/diffraction loss;
- verification against closed forms (dipole, patch antenna, waveguide modes).
Building blocks that exist: the exact voxeliser (fluid solver), the planned FDTD/CPML wave work (M23), the GPU backend, hex meshes.

## 2. Scripting

**Wanted:** scripts to verify results, run time-dependent cases, add effects like rain/path loss (needs 1), and simulate drone aerodynamics.

**Today:** every action is a command; scripts run with `fieldcraft-cli run script.json`; MCP and the JSON control channel let any language drive the app, Python included (docs/mcp.md, docs/control-protocol.md). Transient heat and explicit dynamics exist for time evolution.

**Missing:**
- an official Python package (typed client over the control channel or MCP) with examples: parameter sweeps, loops, post-processing;
- user-defined load/boundary functions of time.

**Drone aerodynamics** builds on the lattice Boltzmann CFD (D3Q19 TRT, wall forces) and still needs rotating propellers (moving/immersed boundaries), turbulence modelling (LES) and fluid–structure coupling (M13).
