title: Octree all-hex: concave transitions and up-front refinement depth
body:
## Observed failure

`mesh.hex.octree` fails on 6 of the 23 corpus parts. Corpus settings: size = 1/25 of the bounding-box diagonal, default `max_depth` 2, cap 500 000 cells.

| part | result |
|---|---|
| i-beam, cantilever-i-beam | `the core's boundary has components of genus [0, 0], the part [0]: the part has walls 2.000 thick, thinner than 3 cells of the deepest level (0.924); use a smaller size, more levels, or a structured (swept) hex mesh` |
| thin-wall-enclosure | same message, walls 1.000 thick, deepest level 0.479 |
| bent-tube | same message, walls 0.984 thick, deepest level 0.536 |
| thin-ribs | `limit reached: the grid needs more than 500000 cells` |
| spline-vase | `limit reached: the grid needs more than 500000 cells` |
| pinhole-block | `octree hex meshing failed after 2 builds: the feature corner at [9.76, 10.18, 10.53] has no vertex; refining for another build needs more than 250000 grid cells` |

The parts that do mesh are refined far more than their geometry needs. The thickness rule (3 cells across every wall) drives the whole 5 mm plate of `analytic-plate-hole` to the finest level everywhere: 163 664 hexes from a requested size of about 8.9 mm. The filleted bracket ends up at a uniform fine size the same way.

![The 200 × 100 × 5 plate with a 20 mm hole, octree all-hex at the corpus size (about 8.9 mm): the thickness rule refines the whole plate to the deepest level, 163 664 hexes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/issue-media/issue-85-plate-octree.png)

![The 8 mm filleted L-bracket, octree all-hex: 30 676 hexes, uniformly at the finest level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/issue-media/issue-85-bracket-octree.png)

## Reproduction

Commit `8caa0d1` (main):

```sh
cargo xtask corpus --part i-beam --no-write
cargo xtask corpus --part thin-wall-enclosure --no-write
cargo xtask corpus --part bent-tube --no-write
cargo xtask corpus --part thin-ribs --no-write
cargo xtask corpus --part spline-vase --no-write
cargo xtask corpus --part pinhole-block --no-write
```

Or from a script, with a part's design written by the corpus tool:

```sh
cargo run --release -p fieldcraft-testkit --bin corpus -- --part i-beam --design i-beam.solidcraft
cat > octree.json <<'EOF'
[{"command": "geometry.open", "params": {"path": "i-beam.solidcraft"}},
 {"command": "mesh.hex.octree", "params": {"max_depth": 2, "max_elements": 2000000}}]
EOF
cargo run --release -p fieldcraft-cli -- run octree.json
```

## Evidence

From the runs above (octree column, wall clock on an Apple M-series laptop):

| part | octree result | octree ms |
|---|---|---|
| i-beam | thin-wall error, first build | 1 402 |
| thin-wall-enclosure | thin-wall error, first build | 2 959 |
| bent-tube | thin-wall error, first build | 605 |
| thin-ribs | 500 000-cell cap | 1 913 |
| spline-vase | 500 000-cell cap | 5 489 |
| pinhole-block | feature corner without a vertex, 2 builds, then the 250 000-cell retry cap | 2 065 |

**One more level makes thin walls mesh, at a cost far out of proportion.** Same script, `max_depth` 3, cap 2 000 000:

| part | `max_depth` 2 | `max_depth` 3 | for comparison: structured sweep (`mesh.hex.generate`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| i-beam | thin-wall error (1.6 s) | **713 728 hexes**, 673 816 grid cells, min scaled Jacobian < 0.001, 305 s | 336 hexes |
| bent-tube | thin-wall error (0.7 s) | **1 183 992 hexes**, 1 533 832 grid cells, min SJ 0.406, 332 s | 192 hexes |
| thin-wall-enclosure | thin-wall error (1.7 s) | `limit reached: the grid needs more than 2000000 cells` | 894 hexes |

## Expected behaviour

- **Depth is chosen up front.** The mesher computes the refinement depth a part needs from its thinnest wall and narrowest patch before it builds anything. It does not fail with "use more levels", and it does not discover the need through rebuilds. When the depth or the cell count that geometry needs is over the caps, it fails at once, naming the wall thickness, the depth it would need and its estimated cell count.
- **Concave refined regions get transition templates** instead of being split out to their orthogonal hull. Curvature can then refine more than one level (`curvature_levels` is 1 today for this reason). Thin and curved parts get graded meshes: fine where the geometry is, coarse inside.
- **References:**
  - R. Schneiders, *Algorithms for quadrilateral and hexahedral mesh generation*, VKI lecture notes 2000, §5 (the modified edge rule);
  - Y. Ito, A. M. Shih, B. K. Soni, *Octree-based reasonable-quality hexahedral mesh generation using a new set of refinement templates*, IJNME 77(13):1809–1833, 2009 (templates for concave edges);
  - M. Livesu, L. Pitzalis, G. Cherchi, *Optimal dual schemes for adaptive grid based hexmeshing*, ACM TOG 41(2):15, 2022, §4.2 (concave transitions) and §6 (weakly balanced grids).

## Investigation

- **Thin walls fail on the first build, without retries.** The thickness rule splits a cell where a wall is thinner than `thickness_cells` (3) cells ([`needs_split`, crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L431-L438](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L431-L438)). When the deepest level still cannot cross a wall, it records the thinnest such wall in `too_thin`. If the core's topology then does not match the part, `build` returns that as a hard error ([#L528-L539](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L528-L539)), so the retry loop ([#L253-L276](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L253-L276)) never runs for it. This issue previously said thin walls "retry up to 4 rebuilds before failing". They do not: they fail at once, and only pinhole-block retries. The depth needed is computable before building: d = ⌈log₃(thickness_cells · h / t_min)⌉ for root size h, from the per-triangle thicknesses that [`triangle_thickness` (#L346)](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L346) already computes.
- **Concave regions are closed by refinement.** After balancing, [`Tree::close` (grid.rs#L204-L238)](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/grid.rs#L204-L238) splits every leaf whose marked-corner pattern has no template. [`templates::classify` (templates.rs#L91-L92)](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/templates.rs#L91-L92) accepts only none / corner / edge / face / full. A leaf at a concave corner of a finer region gets an unsupported pattern, is split, and the split propagates. The module docs state this limit and the upgrade path ([mod.rs#L48-L62](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L48-L62)). This is also why curvature refinement is capped at `curvature_levels` = 1 ([#L428-L430](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L428-L430)).
- **Not yet measured: how much of the count comes from closure and how much from the thickness rule itself.** An isotropic octree must put 3 cells across a wall over the wall's whole area, and concave templates will not change that. Measure it first: count leaves split by `needs_split` and leaves added by `close`, per level, on i-beam (depth 3), bent-tube (depth 3), filleted-bracket and spline-vase. This decides how much each half of the fix buys.
- **pinhole-block has a different cause.** Its failure comes from the feature map ([`map_features`, map.rs#L257](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/map.rs#L257)): a feature corner of a 0.6 mm pinhole gets no core-boundary vertex. Up-front depth from the narrowest patch (`pt.width < 2e` in `needs_split`) should reach the needed level on the first build. If it still fails, split it into its own issue.

## Where to look

- [crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L1-L67](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L1-L67): the pipeline, why 3-refinement templates, and the convex limit.
- [crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L96-L138](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L99-L138): `OctreeOptions` and the defaults (`max_depth` 2, `curvature_levels` 1, `thickness_cells` 3, `attempts` 4).
- [crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L214-L279](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L214-L279): `octree_hex_mesh`, the root size and the retry loop (`RETRY_GROWTH`, `RETRY_MIN_CELLS`).
- [crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L411-L446](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L411-L448): `needs_split`, the size, curvature, thickness and narrow-patch rules.
- [crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L481-L500](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/mod.rs#L481-L500): `tree`, which refines level by level, then hints, then closure.
- [crates/mesh/src/octree/grid.rs](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/grid.rs): the 27-tree, strong balance (`balance_from`), `marks` and `close`, plus the random-tree conformity test.
- [crates/mesh/src/octree/templates.rs](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/octree/templates.rs): the five node-marking templates, in sixths of a leaf on the integer lattice, with exhaustive tests of faces, volume and validity.
- [crates/engine/src/cmd/octree.rs](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/engine/src/cmd/octree.rs): `mesh.hex.octree` (`max_depth` 0..=5).
- [crates/testkit/src/runner.rs#L229-L252](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/testkit/src/runner.rs#L229-L252): the corpus octree column (size, 500 000 cap).
- [docs/meshing/literature.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/meshing/literature.md): section B1. B1.5 Livesu 2022 (dual schemes, §4.2 concave), B1.6 Pitzalis 2021, B1.7 Schneiders (the modified edge rule), B1.8 Ito–Shih–Soni 2009, B1.9 HybridOctree_Hex, B1.10 MCHex. The "Implemented" note records why the dual schemes were not adopted.
- [docs/meshing/corpus.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/meshing/corpus.md): the octree columns.

## Approach

Two parts, in this order.

**1. Up-front depth and budget.**

- Before building the tree, compute the needed depth: the smallest level whose edge e satisfies t_min ≥ `thickness_cells` · e for the thinnest wall, and 2e ≤ the narrowest patch width. Clamp it to the option's cap. Treat `max_depth` as a cap rather than a fixed depth.
- Estimate the leaf count cheaply: the wall area times the cells per area at each level, or a dry run of `needs_split` over the levels without meshing. If it is over `max_elements`, fail at once with the numbers.
- Keep the retry loop for what is genuinely local (feature map, untangling), not for depth.

**2. Concave transitions.** Pick one of these and justify the choice in the module docs and the literature notes:

- (a) **Schneiders' modified edge rule** (VKI notes §5): every edge with a marked end is split in three, with buffer layers in the face templates. This removes the odd-parity patterns (a hexahedron with seven marked corners has 51 boundary quads, which no hex mesh fills, by Mitchell's parity condition). Concave refined regions then close without hull growth. Ito, Shih & Soni 2009 give templates for concave edges, but that paper has not been obtained yet (B1.8). If you use it, get it and cite its sections.
- (b) **The dual schemes of Livesu, Pitzalis & Cherchi 2022**, which are complete for balanced grids, concave transitions included, and also allow weakly balanced grids (§6). The literature notes record why they were not adopted: the reference pipeline's ILP and retried heuristics. A contributor who takes this route must install the schemes deterministically, without an ILP solver. cinolib (MIT) may be read; its TetGen/Triangle wrappers may not.

Either way:

- keep the integer-lattice construction, so shared vertices merge exactly;
- extend the exhaustive template tests (every mask: faces conform, volume exact, every hex valid) and the random-tree conformity test in grid.rs;
- then raise `curvature_levels` toward `max_depth` and re-measure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The needed depth is computed up front. A part whose walls need more depth than the cap fails on the first build with a message giving the thinnest wall, the depth needed and the estimated cells. It never "fails after N builds" for thickness.
- [ ] Transition templates (or dual schemes) cover concave refined regions. The exhaustive template test covers every new pattern, and random balanced trees mesh conforming and valid (extend `random_trees_close_into_conforming_valid_meshes`).
- [ ] The PR reports leaves from the refinement criteria versus leaves added by closure, before and after, for filleted-bracket, spline-vase, analytic-sphere, i-beam and bent-tube.
- [ ] With default options at the corpus size and cap (500 000): i-beam, cantilever-i-beam, bent-tube and spline-vase mesh. thin-wall-enclosure and thin-ribs either mesh, or fail at once with the up-front budget message. Every part that meshes today still meshes, with min scaled Jacobian not lower than today's (docs/meshing/corpus.md).
- [ ] Element counts fall on curved parts that already mesh (analytic-sphere, analytic-torus, filleted-bracket, rounded-box, loft-transition), with the volume error not worse than today.
- [ ] The oracle case `octree-filleted-bracket` passes its reference tolerance. If its mesh changes, the fixture is re-blessed in the PR with the reason (docs/verification.md).
- [ ] Every loop stays capped (closure rounds, cells, attempts), the result is deterministic (same mesh on repeated runs), and hostile options (`max_depth` 5 on a large part, `max_elements` 1) return errors and never panic.
- [ ] `docs/meshing/corpus.md` is regenerated, and the module docs and `docs/meshing/literature.md` are updated: what was adopted and the new limits.

## How to test

```sh
cargo test -p fieldcraft-mesh octree
cargo test -p fieldcraft-engine octree
cargo xtask corpus --part i-beam --no-write            # one part while iterating
cargo xtask corpus --part spline-vase --no-write
cargo xtask corpus                                     # all parts; rewrites docs/meshing/corpus.md
cargo xtask oracle --case octree-filleted-bracket
```

Unit tests go in `crates/mesh/src/octree/tests.rs` and the `grid.rs`/`templates.rs` test modules:

- an L-shaped refined region (a concave corner) closes without splitting outside its bounding box;
- a slab of thickness t gets exactly the computed depth;
- the budget error is immediate.

## Getting started

```sh
git clone https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft && cd fieldcraft
cargo build --release -p fieldcraft-testkit
cargo test -p fieldcraft-mesh
```

The corpus builds its parts with SolidCraft (AGENTS.md, "Test geometry is our own"). Read [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/AGENTS.md) (exact predicates, determinism, bounded loops) first.

---

**Claiming and clean-room rules.** Comment on this issue to claim it. The maintainer assigns it and adds **claimed** ([CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md)). Open a draft PR early with `Closes #85`. Work from the papers cited here only. Permissive code noted in docs/meshing/literature.md (cinolib MIT, HybridOctree_Hex BSD-3) may be read, and anything adapted goes in ATTRIBUTION.md. Never read GPL-family code (CGAL, Gmsh, Netgen, TetGen, …) or code without a licence (Gao et al.'s repository). Never use meshes or results from commercial meshing products.

title: Tet mesh improvement is slow on thin and detailed parts
body:
> **Status: blocked until the tet quality pipeline lands on `main`.** The code this issue is about (`crates/mesh/src/tet/`, the quality options of `mesh.tet.generate`, and the quality columns of the corpus) is in review and not merged yet. On `main` today, `mesh.tet.generate` makes the raw constrained Delaunay tetrahedralization ("no quality refinement yet"). The paths below are the ones the pipeline adds. They become links when it merges, and this note goes away then.

## Observed failure

The tet quality stage (Delaunay refinement, ODT smoothing, then the Klingner–Shewchuk improvement schedule) is slow on thin and detailed parts, and it leaves slivers on several of them:

| part | CDT tets | quality tets | min dihedral | max dihedral | slivers (< 10° or > 170°) CDT → mesh | quality stage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pinhole-block | 96 203 | 933 942 | 7.3° | 172.7° | 65 489 → 165 | **195 s** |
| thin-ribs | 171 | 21 712 | **5.8°** | 174.2° | 141 → **2 867** | 14.2 s |
| shallow-groove | 266 | 13 187 | 8.1° | 171.8° | 85 → 331 | 6.3 s |
| sharp-wedge | 11 | 4 431 | 2.9° | 174.3° | 3 → 34 | 1.2 s |

For comparison, Klingner & Shewchuk report dihedral angles usually between 31° and 149° after their schedule. sharp-wedge's own faces meet at under 3°, so its minimum is bounded by the input. On the other three parts, nothing in the geometry explains the result.

## Reproduction

Run on branch `tet-quality-fc` at commit `5c48616` (pipeline commit on top of `main` `f1253b4`), Apple M-series laptop, release build:

```sh
cargo xtask corpus --part thin-ribs --no-write
cargo xtask corpus --part pinhole-block --no-write
cargo xtask corpus --part shallow-groove --no-write
cargo xtask corpus --part sharp-wedge --no-write
```

The quality columns are `quality tets`, `min dihedral °`, `max dihedral °`, `min radius ratio`, `slivers CDT → mesh`, `quality gate` and `quality ms`. They use the default `QualityOptions` (`crates/testkit/src/runner.rs`, the quality stage).

## Evidence

The table above comes from those four runs. The pinhole-block row took 205.6 s wall clock in total, 195.2 s of it in the quality stage. All four parts pass the validity gate: every element is valid, it just has a poor shape.

**A first profile, thin-ribs** (macOS `sample`, 10 s inside the quality stage, 5 904 main-thread samples). The stage is single-threaded; the other threads are idle.

| inside `tet::improve::improve` (the Klingner–Shewchuk schedule) | samples | share |
|---|---|---|
| `attempt_insert` (composite vertex insertion: Delaunay cavity, smoothing, topological passes, then rollback if no better) | 4 127 | 70 % |
| `topological_pass` (edge removal by Klincsek's DP, multi-face removal) | 1 268 | 21 % |
| `smoothing_pass` (`smooth_vertex`, nonsmooth optimisation) | 478 | 8 % |
| full-mesh scans (`indicators`, `below`) | 7 | < 1 % |

Top self-time functions:

- `tet::measure::quality` plus its inlined array map: about 1 950 samples (33 %);
- `TetComplex::edge_ring_at`: 353;
- `ops::sandwiched_across`: 303;
- malloc/free/realloc together: about 700;
- `ops::klincsek`: 182.

All of the sampled time is in `improve`. Refinement and ODT finished before the window, in the first 3 s. pinhole-block has not been profiled. With 934k tets, refinement and ODT may matter there as well.

## Expected behaviour

Targets, measured with the corpus on one machine before and after, and reported in the PR:

- **Time.** The quality stage is at least 3× faster on pinhole-block and thin-ribs (≤ 65 s and ≤ 5 s on the machine above). No corpus part gets slower.
- **Quality.** On every corpus part, the minimum dihedral angle is no worse than today, and the sliver count is no higher than today. On thin-ribs, shallow-groove and pinhole-block the aim is a minimum dihedral angle ≥ 15°. Sources: Klingner & Shewchuk's reported range; L. A. Freitag, C. Ollivier-Gooch, *Tetrahedral mesh improvement using swapping and smoothing*, IJNME 40(21):3979–4002, 1997, for what swapping plus smoothing reaches. sharp-wedge is bounded by its input angle.
- **Determinism.** The same input gives the same mesh, bit for bit, on every platform and for every thread count (AGENTS.md).

## Investigation

From the code on the branch:

- **The schedule re-evaluates quality from coordinates every time.** `ops::tet_quality` → `measure::quality` (`crates/mesh/src/tet/ops.rs:26`, `crates/mesh/src/tet/measure.rs:82`) has no per-tetrahedron cache. `indicators`, `below`, `smoothing_pass`, `change_quality` and every `star_quality` recompute it (`crates/mesh/src/tet/improve.rs:80-121, 214-288`). That is the 33 % self time.
- **Insertion is the cost.** Each pass, `improve` (`improve.rs:447-501`) sorts all tets by quality and tries `insertion_pass` on the worst 3.5 % (up to `MAX_INSERTION_LIST` = 2000).
  - Each try is `attempt_insert` (`improve.rs:291-333`): up to 4 rounds of `smooth_vertex` plus `topological_pass` over the new vertex's star, smoothing of all its neighbours, `change_quality` over the journal (hash maps), and a rollback when the worst did not improve.
  - Rejected tries cost as much as accepted ones. Nothing remembers that a tetrahedron's neighbourhood already failed and has not changed since, so the next pass tries it again.
- **Smoothing uses numerical gradients.** `smooth_vertex` (`crates/mesh/src/tet/smooth.rs:217`) takes central differences per tetrahedron near the worst (6 quality evaluations each), for up to 8 iterations with up to 6 line-search steps. Klingner & Shewchuk §3.1 and Freitag & Ollivier-Gooch use analytic gradients of the quality measure.
- **Allocation churn.** `star`, `edge_ring_at`, `neighbours` and the journal allocate a fresh `Vec` per call: about 12 % of samples are in the allocator.
- **Quality on thin-ribs.** 2 867 slivers out of 21 712 tets (13 %). Check `ImproveStats` first: did the schedule stop at `max_passes` (10) or `max_insertions`, or after three passes without progress? Then check which tets are left. Are they boundary tets whose vertices are pinned to faces or curves (`VertexKind::Face`/`Curve`), or interior ones? The likely suspects are the 0.8 mm ribs: refinement to the proximity size puts few tets across a rib, and their boundary vertices can only slide on the rib faces.
- **Ruled out by the numbers.** The full-mesh scans are < 1 %, so replacing them alone will not help.

**Profiling plan (do this first, and put the numbers in the PR):**

1. Release build with debug info (the release profile already has `debuginfo`). Profile `corpus --part thin-ribs --no-write` and `--part pinhole-block` with [samply](https://github.com/mstange/samply) (MIT/Apache-2.0), or `perf` on Linux.
2. Split the time by stage: CDT, coarsening, refinement + ODT rounds, `improve`, the final projection onto the B-rep, and tet10. Add `Instant` spans behind the existing report if useful, but leave timing out of deterministic output.
3. Within `improve`, count insertion attempts, accepted and rejected, and the rollback cost. Log `ImproveStats` per pass: worst quality, smoothed, topological and inserted counts, and `stopped`.
4. Re-profile after each change. Keep a before/after table for all 20 corpus parts.

## Where to look

On `main` now:

- [crates/mesh/src/quality/shape.rs](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/quality/shape.rs): element shape measures, including the volume–length measure.
- [crates/mesh/src/quality/mod.rs](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/mesh/src/quality/mod.rs): the validity gate and quality report that the pipeline's output goes through.
- [docs/meshing/literature.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/meshing/literature.md): A3.6 Klingner–Shewchuk, A3.5 ODT and Tournois, and Part D Step 3, the quality plan.
- [docs/meshing/corpus.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/meshing/corpus.md): the corpus parts, their descriptions and categories.

Added by the pipeline (paths and lines at `5c48616`):

- `crates/mesh/src/tet/mod.rs`: the pipeline (module docs list the seven stages), `QualityOptions` (defaults: 3 refinement rounds, 3 ODT passes, improvement on), and `quality_mesh` (line 357).
- `crates/mesh/src/tet/improve.rs`: the schedule. `improve` (447), `attempt_insert` (291), `insertion_pass` (336), `topological_pass` (182), `change_quality` (226), `indicators` (80), `ImproveOptions` (31: `max_passes` 10, `max_insertions` 50 000, `good` sin 40°, `target` sin 30°).
- `crates/mesh/src/tet/smooth.rs`: `smooth_vertex` (217, optimisation-based) and `odt_pass` (123).
- `crates/mesh/src/tet/ops.rs`: edge removal (`remove_edge_at`, `klincsek`), `remove_face`, `insert_delaunay`, `collapse`, `tet_quality`.
- `crates/mesh/src/tet/complex.rs`: `TetComplex` (`star`, `edge_ring_at`, `replace`, `move_point`) and its undo `Journal`.
- `crates/mesh/src/tet/measure.rs`: `quality` (82), the minimum dihedral sine, plus `volume6` and circumcentres.
- `crates/mesh/src/tet/refine.rs`: Delaunay refinement and coarsening.
- `crates/testkit/src/runner.rs`: the corpus quality columns.

## Approach

Speed comes from doing less repeated work, then from cheaper work. Quality comes from the schedule the papers describe:

1. **Cache per-tetrahedron quality** in `TetComplex`, invalidated by `replace`/`move_point` and restored by the journal on rollback. Keep a **worklist** of tets below `good`, updated incrementally. Klingner & Shewchuk §4.2 drive their passes from the tets below a threshold. Then `below`, `indicators` and the sort in `improve` stop rescanning the whole mesh. The thresholded means can be updated incrementally.
2. **Remember failures.** A tetrahedron whose insertion, edge and face removals all failed is not retried until a tetrahedron within its vertices' stars changes. Use a generation counter per vertex. This removes most rejected `attempt_insert` calls.
3. **Cheaper rejection before the composite.** Insertion pays off only when smoothing and topological repair around the new vertex succeed. Estimate the cavity's best case first (for example the Delaunay cavity's tets at the candidate point) and skip candidates that cannot beat the current worst.
4. **Analytic gradients** of the dihedral sine for `smooth_vertex`, with the active-set step of Freitag & Ollivier-Gooch 1997 and Klingner & Shewchuk §3.1. Replace the six evaluations per tetrahedron per iteration.
5. **Order operations as Freitag & Ollivier-Gooch 1997 recommend:** swapping (edge or face removal) before smoothing, and smoothing only vertices of tets below the threshold. They report that the combination reaches its final quality in a few passes.
6. **Reuse buffers.** Give `star`, `edge_ring_at` and `neighbours` caller-provided `Vec`s.
7. **Only then, parallelism.** Operations on vertex-disjoint regions are independent. Process them in independent sets (L. Freitag, M. Jones, P. Plassmann, *An efficient parallel algorithm for mesh smoothing*, IMR 1995) through `fieldcraft-parallel`, with fixed blocks and a fixed order so the result does not depend on the thread count.
8. **Quality on thin parts.** Use the profile's stats to decide between:
   - letting boundary vertices move along faces in the insertion composite (they already move in smoothing);
   - more passes when progress continues (`max_passes` is a cap, not a target);
   - a proximity size that puts at least two tets across a rib.

Sources: B. M. Klingner, J. R. Shewchuk, *Aggressive Tetrahedral Mesh Improvement*, Proc. 16th International Meshing Roundtable, 3–23, 2007, DOI [10.1007/978-3-540-75103-8_1](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-75103-8_1); L. A. Freitag, C. Ollivier-Gooch, IJNME 40(21):3979–4002, 1997; J. R. Shewchuk, *What is a good linear finite element?*, 2002 (the measures). Papers only. Stellar's licence is unverified (see docs/meshing/literature.md), so do not read it, and never read TetGen, CGAL or Gmsh.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The PR includes a profile summary before and after (time per stage, and the top functions) for thin-ribs and pinhole-block.
- [ ] The quality stage is at least 3× faster on pinhole-block and on thin-ribs, on the same machine and the same commit base, as shown by `cargo xtask corpus` before/after. No corpus part is slower than today by more than measurement noise (10 %).
- [ ] Minimum dihedral angle and sliver count are no worse than today on every corpus part. On thin-ribs, shallow-groove and pinhole-block, the minimum dihedral is ≥ 15° (target; report what is reached if the remaining limit is the input geometry).
- [ ] The validity gate passes on all 20 valid corpus parts. Every loop stays bounded and reports when it stops early.
- [ ] Deterministic: the same mesh bit for bit on repeated runs and with 1 and N threads. Add a test that meshes one part twice with different thread counts and compares.
- [ ] Oracle fixtures are unmoved, except cases on tet quality meshes (`filleted-bracket-fillet-stress`, `-coarse`). Those may move only within their reference tolerance and are re-blessed in the PR with the reason.
- [ ] `docs/meshing/corpus.md` is regenerated in the same commit as the change that moves it, and `docs/meshing/literature.md` notes what was adopted.

## How to test

```sh
cargo test -p fieldcraft-mesh tet
```

title: Cook's membrane (finite strain) reference value
body:
## Observed failure

The finite-strain Cook's membrane oracle case [`tests/oracle/nl-cook-membrane`](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/tree/develop/tests/oracle/nl-cook-membrane) is `pending`:

- its reference value is `null`;
- it has no `recipe.json`;
- its `requires` reads "the published finite-strain reference value, transcribed from the paper with its load and material constants".

So FieldCraft's nonlinear solver has no published-benchmark check for nearly incompressible bending at finite strain. The other `nl-*` cases are closed forms.

Correction to the earlier text of this issue: no FieldCraft result for the case is recorded in the repository. "Plane-stress quad8" cannot have produced a nonlinear result, because plane-stress elements are refused in nonlinear steps ([crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L471-L489](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L471-L489)). The case README names hybrid hex20, one element thick in plane strain, and plane-strain quad8. The 25.0 and 25.1 quoted before have no recipe behind them and should not be used.

## Reproduction

Commit `8caa0d1` (main):

```sh
cargo xtask oracle --case nl-cook-membrane     # runs nothing: the case is pending
grep nl-cook-membrane docs/oracle.md           # listed as pending, "to be transcribed"
```

## Evidence

[docs/oracle.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/oracle.md) lists the case as pending, with the quantity "vertical displacement of the top corner C (48, 60) = to be transcribed".

FieldCraft can already solve the model. I built a hybrid hex20 recipe: 16 × 16 × 1, z-symmetry on both faces for plane strain, neo-Hookean with μ = 80.1938 and κ = 400 942 (E = 240.565, ν = 0.4999), and a total dead shear of 32 on the right edge. It converged in 19 increments, with C displaced by (−1.861, 2.443). **These constants and this load are an example only, not a transcribed benchmark.** They show the recipe skeleton below works. They are not a reference.

![Cook's membrane: the tapered panel (0, 0), (48, 44), (48, 60), (0, 44), clamped on x = 0, uniform vertical shear on x = 48, output at C (48, 60)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/issue-media/issue-83-cook-membrane.png)

## Expected behaviour

The case is `active` with a published finite-strain reference value: the vertical displacement of C, cited down to the paper, table (or figure) and mesh. FieldCraft matches it within a tolerance justified by the source's precision and by a mesh-refinement study in the case README.

**About the reference value.** I cannot give you a number I am sure of, so none is given here. The usual finite-strain variant is nearly incompressible neo-Hookean, often quoted with μ = 80.1938 and κ = 40.0942 × 10⁴, but the load magnitude and the tabulated converged value differ between papers. Transcribe them from the paper itself, with its exact constants, load (total force, or traction per length × thickness) and plane-strain assumption. Candidate sources, in order of preference:

1. J. Schröder, T. Wick, S. Reese, P. Wriggers, R. Müller, S. Kollmannsberger, M. Kästner, A. Schwarz, M. Igelbüscher, N. Viebahn, H. R. Bayat, S. Wulfinghoff, K. Mang, E. Rank, T. Bog, D. D'Angella, M. Elhaddad, P. Hennig, A. Düster, W. Garhuom, S. Hubrich, M. Walloth, W. Wollner, C. Kuhn, T. Heister, *A selection of benchmark problems in solid mechanics and applied mathematics*, Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering 28:713–751, 2021, open access. I recall it includes a hyperelastic Cook's membrane with reference values from fine meshes. Confirm the section and table before you use it. **Best choice if it has a table.**
2. J. C. Simo, F. Armero, *Geometrically non-linear enhanced strain mixed methods and the method of incompatible modes*, IJNME 33(7):1413–1449, 1992. This is the source the case cites today. Its Cook's membrane results may be plotted rather than tabulated. A value read off a figure needs a tolerance that covers the reading error, and the README must say so.
3. S. Reese, P. Wriggers, B. D. Reddy, *A new locking-free brick element technique for large deformation problems in elasticity*, Computers & Structures 75(3):291–304, 2000; S. Glaser, F. Armero, *On the formulation of enhanced strain finite elements in finite deformations*, Engineering Computations 14(7):759–791, 1997. Both are cross-checks, if they use the same constants and load.

The geometry is R. D. Cook, *Improved two-dimensional finite element*, J. Struct. Div. ASCE 100(ST9):1851–1863, 1974. Only published numbers are used. Never use a value from a commercial code's manual or output (AGENTS.md, Verification).

## Investigation

- The case files are [`expected.json`](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/tests/oracle/nl-cook-membrane/expected.json) and [`README.md`](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/tests/oracle/nl-cook-membrane/README.md). There is no recipe or fixture yet.
- **Element choice.**
  - ν ≈ 0.4999 needs a mixed element. Use hybrid hex20, one element thick, with symmetry on both z faces. That is the Simo–Taylor–Pister form ([docs/fem.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/fem.md), "Nonlinear static analysis"), and it needs the neo-Hookean option, which matches the benchmark.
  - 2D hybrid elements do not exist. Plane-strain quad8 is a displacement element and locks near incompressibility, so use it only for a compressible variant, if the source has one.
- **The load is a dead load.** A `force` with the default `"distribution": "total"` is split by area over the loaded face, which matches a uniform traction. If the source specifies a follower load, say so and do not use this case.
- **Not checked yet: mesh convergence.** Run 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 divisions per side and show the convergence in the README (docs/verification.md, "Adding cases", point 2).

## Where to look

- [tests/oracle/nl-cook-membrane/](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/tree/develop/tests/oracle/nl-cook-membrane): the pending case.
- [tests/oracle/nl-cylinder-inflation/recipe.json](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/tests/oracle/nl-cylinder-inflation/recipe.json): a nearly incompressible neo-Hookean hybrid hex20 recipe with z-symmetry, the model to copy.
- [tests/oracle/nl-elastica-cantilever/expected.json](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/tests/oracle/nl-elastica-cantilever/expected.json): how a `solve.probe` measure, tolerance and reason are written.
- [docs/verification.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/verification.md): the case format, and how a pending case becomes active.
- [docs/fem.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/fem.md) (verification paragraph of "Nonlinear static analysis") and [docs/solvers/literature.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/solvers/literature.md) (Parts L and M): both say the case is pending. Update them.

## Approach

1. Get the paper and transcribe: material constants, load (total force and how it is applied), thickness or plane-strain assumption, quantity (vertical displacement of C), the reference value, and where it comes from (table or figure, page, mesh). Write all of it in `source` and in the README.
2. Write `recipe.json` from the skeleton below with the transcribed constants and load. E and ν follow from μ and κ: E = 9κμ/(3κ + μ), ν = (3κ − 2μ)/(2(3κ + μ)). FieldCraft's neo-Hookean takes μ and κ from E and ν (docs/fem.md).
3. Run a mesh study. Choose the mesh that is converged well inside the tolerance, or the mesh the source prescribes if it compares at one mesh.
4. Set the tolerance from the source's precision: a tabulated converged value with 3 to 4 significant digits supports about 0.5 %, and a value read from a figure needs more. Give the reason. Never widen a tolerance to make the case pass. If FieldCraft misses, keep the honest tolerance and add `known_failure`.

Recipe skeleton. The `vector` and material values are placeholders until transcribed:

```json
[
 {"command": "mesh.block", "params": {"body": "Cook", "kind": "hex20",
   "corners": [[0,0,0],[48,44,0],[48,60,0],[0,44,0],[0,0,1],[48,44,1],[48,60,1],[0,44,1]],
   "divisions": [16, 16, 1], "faces": {"6": "clamp", "4": "load", "1": "z0", "2": "z1"}}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "all", "geometry": [{"body": "Cook"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "clamp", "geometry": [{"body": "Cook", "face": "clamp"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "load", "geometry": [{"body": "Cook", "face": "load"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "z0", "geometry": [{"body": "Cook", "face": "z0"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "z1", "geometry": [{"body": "Cook", "face": "z1"}]}},
 {"command": "model.material.create", "params": {"name": "Rubber", "elastic": {"type": "isotropic", "young": "E", "poisson": "ν"}, "hyperelastic": {"type": "neo_hookean"}}},
 {"command": "model.section.create", "params": {"name": "panel", "set": "all", "material": "Rubber", "kind": {"type": "solid"}, "formulation": {"hybrid": true}}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "fix", "type": "fixed", "target": {"set": "clamp"}}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "pz0", "type": "symmetry", "target": {"set": "z0"}, "plane": "z"}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "pz1", "type": "symmetry", "target": {"set": "z1"}, "plane": "z"}},
 {"command": "model.load.create", "params": {"name": "F", "type": "force", "target": {"set": "load"}, "vector": [0, "F", 0]}},
 {"command": "model.step.create", "params": {"name": "Shear", "procedure": {"type": "nonlinear_static"}, "boundary_conditions": ["fix", "pz0", "pz1"], "loads": ["F"]}},
 {"command": "solve.nonlinear", "params": {"step": "Shear"}, "id": "solve"}
]
```

Measure: `{"command": "solve.probe", "params": {"step": "Shear", "at": [[48, 60, 0]]}, "pointer": "/nodes/0/displacement/1"}`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `tests/oracle/nl-cook-membrane/expected.json` has `"kind": "benchmark"`, no `status`/`requires`, and `source` citing the paper, table or figure, page and mesh. `value` is the transcribed number, and the tolerance comes with its reason.
- [ ] `recipe.json` uses the transcribed constants and load. The README gives the model, the mesh study (at least 4 meshes) and how the value was transcribed.
- [ ] `cargo xtask oracle --case nl-cook-membrane` passes (or the case is marked `known_failure` with the reason), and `fixture.json` is blessed.
- [ ] Every other oracle fixture is unmoved.
- [ ] docs/oracle.md, the verification paragraph in docs/fem.md and docs/solvers/literature.md Parts L–M no longer say "pending".
- [ ] No number comes from a commercial code's documentation or output.

## How to test

```sh
cargo run --release -p fieldcraft-cli -- run tests/oracle/nl-cook-membrane/recipe.json   # the model solves
cargo xtask oracle --case nl-cook-membrane
cargo xtask oracle --bless nl-cook-membrane     # once it passes
cargo xtask oracle                              # full run; regenerates docs/oracle.md
```

## Getting started

```sh
git clone https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft && cd fieldcraft
cargo build --release -p fieldcraft-cli
```

No Rust changes are needed. This is a good first verification task. Read [docs/verification.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/verification.md) and the "Verification and validation" section of [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/AGENTS.md).

Never copy input files, text or figures, never run or take values from commercial CAE products, and never read GPL-family code (deal.II, MOOSE, CalculiX, Code_Aster, …).

title: Incompatible-mode hex8 and quad4 in nonlinear steps
body:
## Observed failure

A nonlinear step refuses every incompatible-mode element (hex8 and quad4, `"formulation": {"incompatible_modes": true}`):

```
Error: step 16 (solve.nonlinear): element 1: not supported yet: hex8 incompatible modes in nonlinear steps (their finite-strain form, enhanced assumed strain, is not implemented; use full integration, hybrid or hex20)
```

The same elements are also refused without nonlinear geometry when the material is plastic ("with an inelastic material (their internal modes would carry the plastic history …"). 2D quad4 gives "2D quad4 incompatible modes in nonlinear steps …".

So the cheap bending element FieldCraft offers for linear analysis cannot be used for large deflection or plasticity. The alternatives are full-integration hex8, which locks in bending (numbers below), hybrid elements, or quadratic elements at several times the cost.

## Reproduction

Commit `8caa0d1` (main). Take the oracle case [`nl-elastica-cantilever`](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/tree/develop/tests/oracle/nl-elastica-cantilever) (L = 10, b = 1, h = 0.5, E = 10⁴, ν = 0, four dead tip loads) and mesh it with 40 × 1 × 1 hex8, one element through the depth:

```sh
R=tests/oracle/nl-elastica-cantilever/recipe.json
CORNERS='[[0,0,0],[10,0,0],[10,1,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0.5],[10,0,0.5],[10,1,0.5],[0,1,0.5]]'
# incompatible modes: refused
jq --argjson c "$CORNERS" '.[0].params += {kind: "hex8", divisions: [40,1,1], corners: $c}
   | .[5].params.formulation = {incompatible_modes: true}' $R > elastica-hex8-im.json
cargo run --release -p fieldcraft-cli -- run elastica-hex8-im.json
# full integration: solves, but locks
jq --argjson c "$CORNERS" '.[0].params += {kind: "hex8", divisions: [40,1,1], corners: $c}' $R > elastica-hex8-full.json
```

Read the tip displacement with `solve.probe` (`{"step": "K1", "at": [[10,0,0],[10,0,0.5]]}`, averaged) after each step, for example through `fieldcraft-cli mcp --headless` and its `batch` tool.

## Evidence

Full-integration hex8, 40 × 1 × 1, against the elastica values in the oracle case (Bisshopp–Drucker, Mattiasson's table). I ran this on `8caa0d1`:

| P L²/(E I) | δ_v/L hex8 full | elastica | error | δ_h/L hex8 full | elastica | error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.2737 | 0.301721 | −9.3 % | 0.0462 | 0.056433 | −18.2 % |
| 2 | 0.4606 | 0.493457 | −6.7 % | 0.1380 | 0.160642 | −14.1 % |
| 5 | 0.6935 | 0.713792 | −2.8 % | 0.3583 | 0.387628 | −7.6 % |
| 10 | 0.8009 | 0.810609 | −1.2 % | 0.5317 | 0.554996 | −4.2 % |

With ν = 0 this is pure shear locking. The same mesh with incompatible modes is refused as shown above. In a linear step the incompatible-mode hex8 is within 0.5 % of Timoshenko on a coarse cantilever (oracle case [`cantilever-hex8-incompatible`](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/tree/develop/tests/oracle/cantilever-hex8-incompatible)).

## Expected behaviour

The incompatible-mode (enhanced assumed strain, EAS) hex8 and quad4 solve nonlinear steps, as in J. C. Simo, F. Armero, *Geometrically non-linear enhanced strain mixed methods and the method of incompatible modes*, IJNME 33(7):1413–1449, 1992:

- The 40 × 1 × 1 elastica above is within 1 % of the elastica at all four loads, for both δ_v and δ_h. This tolerance is a target to confirm with a refinement study in the case README. Full hex8 is 9.3 % off.
- At small load, the result equals the linear incompatible-mode solution.
- The element passes the nonlinear patch test on the distorted mesh of `nl-patch-hex8`.
- In large compression of nearly incompressible material, spurious hourglass modes (Wriggers & Reese 1996) are either stabilised or detected. The step must never return a converged result that has silently hourglassed.

## Investigation

- **Where it is refused.** In the element kernels, before any assembly:
  - 3D: [`Solid::check_nonlinear`, crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L238-L256](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L238-L256);
  - 2D: [`Plane::check_nonlinear`, #L471-L489](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L471-L489);
  - the reasons are written up in the module docs, [#L57-L62](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L57-L62).
- **Why it is not a one-line change.** The linear element condenses its 9 modes (hex8) or 4 modes (quad4) statically, once ([`Solid::stiffness`, crates/fem/src/element.rs#L385-L406](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/element.rs#L385-L406)). In a nonlinear step the modes α enter F, so the element residual depends on α. α must either be solved for at each evaluation or be carried from one Newton iteration to the next.
- **The solver's element contract.** The solver evaluates each element as a pure function of (u, committed history) and returns an `updated` history ([`Problem::element`, crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L293-L307](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L293-L307)). That history is committed only when an increment converges ([#L951](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L951)) and is sized integration points × material history ([#L864-L869](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L864-L869), checked by [`check_history`, finite.rs#L228-L234](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L228-L234)). Nothing survives between two iterations of one increment. Iteration-to-iteration storage of α would mean new solver state that cut-backs must also discard.
- **What already exists.** The mapped mode gradients, det J₀/det J · J₀⁻¹ ∂P/∂ξ (Taylor, Beresford & Wilson 1976), are in [`incompatible_gradients`, element.rs#L343-L355](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/element.rs#L343-L355) and [`centre_jacobian`, #L357-L360](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/element.rs#L357-L360). The 2D version, with the Wilson–Ibrahimbegovic mean shift for axisymmetry, is in [`Plane::incompatible_columns`, crates/fem/src/plane.rs#L345-L392](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/plane.rs#L345-L392). These are exactly the gradients the enhanced deformation gradient needs.
- **Ruled out.**
  - Reduced-integration hex8 with hourglass control. It is a different element, and it is already planned for explicit dynamics.
  - Silently falling back to full integration. That would give the user the locking numbers in the table above under the element they did not ask for.
- **Check first.** Decide where α lives. My recommendation is in Approach (option A), because it keeps the solver contract unchanged. Then confirm that `check_history`, the committed-history sizing and `nonlinear_stresses` can carry an extra per-element block after the per-point material history.

## Where to look

- [crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L1-L62](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/finite.rs#L1-L62): the total Lagrangian loops (f_a = ∫ Bₓ,aᵀ τ dV₀, K_ab material plus geometric), which the modes join as extra "nodes".
- [crates/fem/src/element.rs#L362-L383](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/element.rs#L362-L383): `incompatible_parts` (K_uu, K_uα, K_αα), the linear version of the blocks you will build.
- [crates/fem/src/plane.rs#L394](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/plane.rs#L394): `full_stiffness`, the 2D counterpart.
- [crates/fem/src/dof.rs#L183-L188](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/dof.rs#L183-L188): `Internal`, which counts the condensed unknowns.
- [crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L330-L345](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L330-L345): `evaluate`, which collects each element's updated history.
- [crates/solver/tests/plasticity.rs#L208-L212](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/tests/plasticity.rs#L208-L212): the current refusal test with a plastic material.
- [docs/fem.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/fem.md) (element table under "Nonlinear static analysis") and [docs/solvers/literature.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/solvers/literature.md) Part M: to update.

## Approach

Sources (papers only):

- J. C. Simo, F. Armero, IJNME 33(7):1413–1449, 1992. The enhanced deformation gradient, and the incompatible-mode element as its special case.
- J. C. Simo, F. Armero, R. L. Taylor, *Improved versions of assumed enhanced strain tri-linear elements for 3D finite deformation problems*, CMAME 110(3–4):359–386, 1993. The 3D element and its mode sets.
- P. Wriggers, S. Reese, *A note on enhanced strain methods for large deformations*, CMAME 135(3–4):201–209, 1996. The hourglass instability in compression.
- Stabilisation:
  - S. Glaser, F. Armero, *On the formulation of enhanced strain finite elements in finite deformations*, Engineering Computations 14(7):759–791, 1997;
  - S. Reese, P. Wriggers, B. D. Reddy, *A new locking-free brick element technique for large deformation problems in elasticity*, Computers & Structures 75(3):291–304, 2000.

**Kinematics.** F = I + Σ_a u_a ⊗ ∇₀N_a + Σ_k α_k ⊗ ∇̃N_k, where ∇̃N_k are today's mapped mode gradients (det J₀/det J · J₀⁻ᵀ ∂P_k/∂ξ). In the current configuration ∇ₓÑ_k = F⁻ᵀ ∇̃N_k. Everything downstream of F (material, Kirchhoff stress τ, spatial tangent c) is unchanged.

**Residuals and tangent.** These are the same loops as `finite.rs`, with the modes as extra columns:

- r_u = ∫ Bₓᵀ τ dV₀ − f_ext
- h = ∫ B̃ₓᵀ τ dV₀ = 0, element by element
- K_uu, K_uα, K_αu, K_αα = ∫ (Bᵀ c B + ∇ₓN · τ ∇ₓN I) dV₀ over the (u, α) pairs, geometric term included
- after condensation: K* = K_uu − K_uα K_αα⁻¹ K_αu and f* = r_u − K_uα K_αα⁻¹ h

**Where α lives. Option A (recommended).** Store α_n, the last converged value, in the element's committed history, after the material blocks. At every evaluation, solve h(u, α) = 0 for α by a local Newton iteration that starts from α_n:

- α ← α − K_αα⁻¹ h;
- bound the iteration count and tolerance, and return `Error::Degenerate` naming the element if it does not converge;
- K_αα must stay positive definite, or the iteration fails and the increment cuts back.

At the converged α, h = 0, so f* = r_u, and K* is the consistent tangent by the implicit function theorem. The element stays a pure function of (u, committed history), cut-backs need nothing new, and the converged α goes into `updated`.

The material history at the points must be the one evaluated at the converged α. For plasticity, every local iteration starts the material from `committed`. That also lifts the small-strain refusal for inelastic materials.

**Option B.** Simo & Armero's update α ← α − K_αα⁻¹(h + K_αu Δu), carried across global iterations. It is cheaper per evaluation, but it needs a per-iteration state in `Run` that the solver keeps separate from `committed` and drops on a cut-back. Only take this route with a measured reason.

**Hourglassing.** Build the case first: a block in large compression (stretch ≤ 0.6) with a nearly incompressible neo-Hookean material, where Wriggers & Reese report the spurious modes. Watch for loss of positive definiteness, or a converged state with hourglass patterns. Then add one of the published remedies:

- Glaser & Armero 1997's modified enhanced gradient;
- or Reese–Wriggers–Reddy's stabilisation.

Document which one, and what its parameters are, in the module docs. If neither is adopted in this PR, the solver must detect the instability (non-positive-definite element K* at a converged state) and stop with an error naming the element. A warning is not enough.

**2D quad4.** The same, with 4 modes. For axisymmetry keep the mean-shifted hoop column. Plane stress stays refused (a separate limitation).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Incompatible-mode hex8 and quad4 (plane strain, axisymmetric) solve nonlinear steps with any material the full element supports: St Venant–Kirchhoff, neo-Hookean, Mooney–Rivlin/Yeoh, J2 with finite and small strain. The two refusals in `finite.rs` and the plasticity refusal test are rewritten.
- [ ] Element tangent (condensed K*) matches central differences of the condensed forces (with α re-solved) to the tolerance the other elements use in `finite.rs`. Check from an elastic state and from a plastic history.
- [ ] Linear limit: at a load factor of 10⁻⁶ × the `cantilever-hex8-incompatible` load, the nonlinear tip displacement over the load equals the linear incompatible-mode result to 1e-6 relative.
- [ ] Nonlinear patch test on the distorted `nl-patch-hex8` mesh, incompatible modes: exact to the patch tolerance.
- [ ] New oracle case `nl-elastica-cantilever-hex8-incompatible` (kind `theory`): 40 × 1 × 1 hex8 IM, values from `nl-elastica-cantilever/expected.json`. The tolerance is set from a refinement study shown in its README (target 1 %), with its reason.
- [ ] Hourglass case: a compression test in `crates/solver/tests/` that either converges to the homogeneous solution (stabilised) or stops with a named error. It never converges to a hourglassed state.
- [ ] The local α iteration is bounded (constant documented) and reports non-convergence as an element error. A hostile-input test (inverted element, non-finite displacement) returns `Err` and never panics.
- [ ] Every existing oracle fixture is unmoved. In particular `cantilever-hex8-incompatible`, `patch-hex8-incompatible` and all `nl-*` cases are bit-identical.
- [ ] docs/fem.md (element table), docs/solvers/literature.md Part M, the `finite.rs` module docs and `docs/oracle.md` are updated.

## How to test

```sh
cargo test -p fieldcraft-fem finite
cargo test -p fieldcraft-solver --test nonlinear --test plasticity
cargo xtask oracle --case nl-elastica-cantilever-hex8-incompatible --case cantilever-hex8-incompatible --case nl-patch-hex8
cargo xtask oracle --bless nl-elastica-cantilever-hex8-incompatible   # once it passes
```

The new case follows docs/verification.md:

- `recipe.json`: the elastica recipe with `"kind": "hex8"`, `"divisions": [40, 1, 1]`, the corners above, and `"formulation": {"incompatible_modes": true}` on the section. Probe the two tip nodes (10, 0, 0) and (10, 0, 0.5) and average them, or probe (10, 0, 0.25) if `solve.probe` interpolates there.
- `expected.json`: the eight quantities of `nl-elastica-cantilever`, with tolerance and reason.

## Getting started

```sh
git clone https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft && cd fieldcraft
cargo build -p fieldcraft-cli
cargo test -p fieldcraft-fem -p fieldcraft-solver
```

Read [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/AGENTS.md) (no panics, bounded loops, determinism) and [docs/verification.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/verification.md) first. Cook's membrane (#83) is a natural second benchmark for the 2D element once its reference is in.

title: Kinematic hardening at finite strain
body:
## Observed failure

A nonlinear static step with nonlinear geometry refuses any material with bilinear **kinematic** hardening:

```
error: step 14 (solve.nonlinear): not supported yet: the kinematic hardening of material `Steel` at finite strain (its back stress is not coaxial with the elastic stretch, which the exponential return map needs); use nonlinear_geometry false or isotropic hardening in nonlinear steps (step `Pull`)
```

Today you can have kinematic hardening (the Bauschinger effect, cyclic plasticity, ratcheting) **or** large deformation in an implicit step, but not both. Small strain works (`nonlinear_geometry: false`, oracle case [`j2-bauschinger`](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/tree/develop/tests/oracle/j2-bauschinger)). Explicit dynamics is not affected: it uses its own hypoelastic update.

## Reproduction

Commit `8caa0d1` (main). This is the `j2-bauschinger` oracle recipe with `nonlinear_geometry` switched on: a unit hex8 cube on symmetry planes, E = 200 000, ν = 0.3, σ_y = 250, H = 2000 kinematic, pulled along x and brought back to zero on a load path.

```sh
jq '(.[] | select(.command == "model.step.create") | .params.procedure.nonlinear_geometry) = true' \
  tests/oracle/j2-bauschinger/recipe.json > kinematic-finite.json
cargo run --release -p fieldcraft-cli -- run kinematic-finite.json
```

## Evidence

The error above, from that command. Two checks refuse it:

- the solver refuses the step before it assembles anything: [`plasticity()` in crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L720-L724](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L720-L724);
- the material point refuses it too, so no other caller can get round the solver check: [`finite_isochoric` in crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L118-L124](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L118-L124).

Tests pin both refusals: [crates/solver/tests/plasticity.rs#L206](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/tests/plasticity.rs#L206) and [crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L395-L396](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L395-L396).

## Expected behaviour

The step solves, and gives these results:

1. **Proportional (coaxial) paths match the small-strain closed form, using log strain and Kirchhoff stress.** In the logarithmic-strain-space model of Miehe, Apel & Lambrecht (2002), a uniaxial path whose principal axes do not rotate is the 1D small-strain model with ε → ln λ and σ → τ (Kirchhoff). Take the cube pulled to a log strain ε_a = 0.2 (displacement e^0.2 − 1 = 0.2214028) and brought back to zero on the path `[[0, 0], [0.5, 1], [1, 0]]`. The residual Kirchhoff stress is then
   τ_res = σ_a − 2σ_y − E_t (ε_a − 2σ_y/E) = −σ_y (1 − E_t/E) = **−247.5247525**,
   with E_t = EH/(E + H) = 1980.198. The answer does not depend on ε_a once the path yields in reverse. The probe reports Cauchy stress, σ = τ/J with ln J = τ/(3K), so σ_xx = **−247.6473198**. The accumulated equivalent plastic strain is (σ_a − σ_y)/H + E/(E + H)(ε_a − 2σ_y/E) = **0.3923267**. For comparison, isotropic hardening would yield again only at −σ_a.
2. **Simple shear to large γ (≥ 5) gives no stress oscillation.** The shear stress rises monotonically under linear kinematic hardening. Hypoelastic Jaumann-rate models oscillate here: J. C. Nagtegaal, J. E. de Jong, *Some aspects of non-isotropic workhardening in finite strain plasticity*, in E. H. Lee, R. L. Mallett (eds.), Plasticity of Metals at Finite Strain, Stanford/RPI 1982, 65–102. A formulation in logarithmic strain space has no such oscillation by construction.
3. **Isotropic hardening is unchanged.** Every existing plasticity fixture (`nl-j2-uniaxial`, `plastic-thick-cylinder`, `plastic-hinge-cantilever`, `j2-heated-bar`, `j2-bauschinger`) stays inside its band.

## Investigation

- **Why it is refused.** The finite-strain J2 model is Simo's multiplicative model: bₑ = F Cₚ⁻¹ Fᵀ with a Hencky energy, returned in the principal frame of the trial bₑ ([elastoplastic.rs#L8-L37](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L8-L37)). That return builds its trial deviator from the three principal log strains only ([#L125-L132](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L125-L132)). A back stress α is a full symmetric tensor that is generally not coaxial with bₑ, so ξ = s − α has off-diagonal terms in that frame and the principal-frame return is no longer exact. The refusal is correct. The fix needs a formulation where α lives in a fixed frame.
- **What already fits.** The history layout reserves values 6–11 for the back stress ([#L48-L50](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L48-L50), `HISTORY = 13`). At finite strain those slots are unused today. The small-strain path ([`small`, #L192-L217](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L192-L217)) already runs the full tensor radial return with α through [`J2::radial_return`](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/plasticity.rs#L289) and its algorithmic tangent [`J2::tangent`](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/plasticity.rs#L322). In Miehe's log-space model the return **is** that small-strain return, applied to E = ½ ln C. Most of the work is the kinematic wrapper around it, not a new return map.
- **Ruled out.** A hypoelastic (Jaumann or Green–Naghdi) rate in the implicit path. It oscillates in simple shear with kinematic hardening (Nagtegaal & de Jong 1982), it is not hyperelastic, and it would split implicit plasticity into two families.
- **Check first.** Whether `MaterialModel::response` ([crates/fem/src/constitutive.rs#L209-L234](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/constitutive.rs#L209-L234)) can route kinematic J2 to a new function while isotropic J2 keeps `finite_isochoric`. That keeps every existing fixture bit-identical. Also check how hybrid elements split the response (isochoric part plus `volumetric`), because the new path has to fit that split too.

## Where to look

- [crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L114-L177](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L114-L177): `finite_isochoric`, the current finite-strain material point (Kirchhoff stress plus spatial tangent). The new function sits beside it.
- [crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L179-L217](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L179-L217): `volumetric` and `small`, the return to reuse on log strains.
- [crates/fem/src/plasticity.rs#L1-L40](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/plasticity.rs#L1-L40): the radial return with Prager's rule, α ← α + √(2/3) H_k Δε_p n.
- [crates/fem/src/constitutive.rs#L103](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/constitutive.rs#L103) `push_forward` and [#L350](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/constitutive.rs#L350) `logarithmic_strain`: the existing push-forward of a material tangent and the log strain.
- [crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L244-L276](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/fem/src/elastoplastic.rs#L244-L276): `check_finite_tangent`, the central-difference tangent check to reuse.
- [crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L697-L733](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/src/nonlinear.rs#L697-L734): `plasticity()`, where the solver-level refusal comes out.
- [crates/solver/tests/plasticity.rs#L117](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/solver/tests/plasticity.rs#L117): the small-strain Bauschinger test, the model for the finite-strain one.
- [docs/fem.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/fem.md) ("Nonlinear static analysis") and [docs/solvers/literature.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/solvers/literature.md) (Part N): the documentation to update.

## Approach

Implement additive plasticity in the Lagrangian logarithmic strain space: C. Miehe, N. Apel, M. Lambrecht, *Anisotropic additive plasticity in the logarithmic strain space: modular kinematic formulation and implementation based on incremental minimization principles for standard materials*, CMAME 191(47–48):5383–5425, 2002, DOI [10.1016/S0045-7825(02)00438-3](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0045-7825(02)00438-3). Background: J. C. Simo, T. J. R. Hughes, *Computational Inelasticity*, Springer 1998, §3.3 (the return) and ch. 9.

There are three modules.

1. **Geometric pre-processor.** C = FᵀF = Σ λ_a² N_a ⊗ N_a (`dense::symmetric_eigen`), and E = ½ ln C = Σ ln λ_a N_a ⊗ N_a.
2. **Constitutive module, exactly the small-strain model.** The history is Eₚ (values 0–5, engineering shears as in `small`), α (6–11) and ε̄ₚ (12). The trial is E − Eₚ,ₙ. Call `small(j2, &E, …)`, which returns the stress **T** (work-conjugate to E) and the algorithmic modulus 𝔼 = ∂T/∂E from `J2::tangent`. Prager's rule in log space is unchanged.
3. **Geometric post-processor.**
   - S = T : ℙ with ℙ = 2 ∂E/∂C.
   - ℂ = ℙᵀ : 𝔼 : ℙ + T : 𝕃 with 𝕃 = 4 ∂²E/∂C∂C.
   - In the eigenbasis of C, with e_a = ln λ_a, d_a = λ_a⁻², f_a = −2λ_a⁻⁴: ℙ = Σ_a d_a M_aa ⊗ M_aa + Σ_{a≠b} θ_ab (M_ab ⊗ M_ab + M_ab ⊗ M_ba), with θ_ab = (e_a − e_b)/(λ_a² − λ_b²) → d_a/2 as λ_b → λ_a. M_ab = N_a ⊗ N_b.
   - 𝕃 has the analogous spectral form with second divided differences. The paper gives both, with the limits for coincident eigenvalues.
   - Make these limits smooth the way `log_divided_difference` already does (a series near r = 0). Uniaxial and undeformed states are the common case, not an edge case.
   - Push forward for the element loops: τ = F S Fᵀ, c = `push_forward(F)` applied to ℂ.

Notes:

- **Hybrid elements** need the isochoric/volumetric split. Here J2 is pressure insensitive and Eₚ is deviatoric, so tr E = ln J carries all the volume. Use the deviatoric return (`bulk = false`) on dev E and the existing `volumetric` U(J) = K/2 (ln J)². Verify it against the full element on a compressible case.
- **Scope.** Route only **kinematic** hardening to the new path. For isotropic hardening on proportional paths the two models agree exactly, but on rotating paths they differ slightly. Keeping isotropic on Simo's model keeps every existing fixture bit-identical.
- Lift the two refusals, and update docs/fem.md, docs/solvers/literature.md (Part N: implemented, no longer "the route when it comes") and the module docs, citing the paper.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Kinematic hardening with `nonlinear_geometry: true` solves for every continuum element that supports J2 today: tet4, tet10, wedge6, hex8, hex20 full and reduced, hybrid hex8/hex20/tet10, plane strain and axisymmetric.
- [ ] Material-point tangent matches central differences to 1e-7 (relative to the largest entry), elastic and plastic, from a committed plastic history with α ≠ 0, at small, large and uniaxial (two equal stretches) deformations. Reuse `check_finite_tangent`.
- [ ] Element tangents match central differences of element forces, as for the existing materials in `crates/fem/src/finite.rs`.
- [ ] New oracle case `nl-j2-bauschinger` (kind `theory`) is active. It uses the recipe above with ε_a = 0.2 and checks σ_xx = −247.6473198 (relative 1e-6) and ε̄ₚ = 0.3923267 (relative 1e-6). Reason: a homogeneous state the element represents exactly, and the exponential map integrates a proportional path exactly.
- [ ] Simple shear of one hex8 to γ = 5 in at least 50 increments: τ_xy rises monotonically, with no oscillation. Make this a solver test.
- [ ] Newton converges quadratically in a plastic cantilever with kinematic hardening at finite strain: measured order > 1.8, the way `plastic_newton_converges_quadratically` measures it.
- [ ] Every existing oracle fixture is unmoved (`cargo xtask oracle` shows no fixture change), and isotropic J2 results are bit-identical.
- [ ] The refusal tests are rewritten to assert the solve succeeds. The Johnson–Cook rate refusal stays.
- [ ] docs/fem.md, docs/solvers/literature.md, the module docs and `docs/oracle.md` are updated.

## How to test

```sh
cargo test -p fieldcraft-fem elastoplastic
cargo test -p fieldcraft-fem finite
cargo test -p fieldcraft-solver --test plasticity
cargo xtask oracle --case nl-j2-bauschinger --case j2-bauschinger --case nl-j2-uniaxial
cargo xtask oracle --bless nl-j2-bauschinger      # only once it passes
```

New oracle case layout (docs/verification.md):

- `tests/oracle/nl-j2-bauschinger/recipe.json`: copy `j2-bauschinger/recipe.json`, set the displacement to `0.22140275816016985`, set `"nonlinear_geometry": true`, and keep increments ≤ 0.05.
- `expected.json`: `"kind": "theory"`, with `source` citing Miehe, Apel & Lambrecht 2002 and Prager 1955 and giving the closed form above. The quantities are `residual_stress` (`/elements/0/stress/0/0`) and `plastic_strain` (`/elements/0/plastic_strain/0`), each with a tolerance and a reason.
- `README.md`: the model and the formula. `fixture.json` comes from `--bless`.

## Getting started

```sh
git clone https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft && cd fieldcraft
cargo build -p fieldcraft-cli
cargo test -p fieldcraft-fem -p fieldcraft-solver
```

Read [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/AGENTS.md) (no panics, bounded loops, determinism) and [docs/verification.md](https://github.com/jyviko/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/verification.md) before you start.

title: Release builds: macOS app, Linux and Windows binaries from CI
body: Testers today need Rust and `cargo run --release -p fieldcraft`. Build signed release artifacts in CI from a `release` branch (macOS .app/.dmg, Linux, Windows .zip), publish them as a GitHub release draft, verify, then publish. Includes the app icon family already in `assets/app-icon` and the licences file.
